Breaking: This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Binary stars are common in the Milky Way.
  • Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs).
  • Recent findings suggest that it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

Recent findings suggest that it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

In a recent development, the common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

It has been revealed that this simple graphic highlights how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112.

It has been revealed that this is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

It has been revealed that observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in newly introduced research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

"The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag.".

Industry observers note that that much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

It has been revealed that astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

In a recent development, âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â said first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â.

In a recent development, stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.).

Observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

According to recent reports, âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â stated co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â.

Industry observers note that âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â mentioned co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Upcoming York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â.

This was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

This is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel highlights the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026).

Industry observers note that since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an vital role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

As in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an important role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

Industry observers note that that work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

Sources indicate that the modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

According to recent reports, the astronomers called the pair Massive Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

In a recent development, these artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel highlights the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia).

"The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

According to recent reports, "In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory says that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

In a recent development, but this work opens a new window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

According to recent reports, this work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

Latest Update: Apple Galette

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • What People Are Saying:“I've already made this twice.
  • It has been revealed that first, combine the apples, brown sugar, lemon juice, cinnamon, and salt in a large bowl.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honestly, we can’t think of anything better than a galette. They've got all the delicious elements of pie—flaky, buttery crust and tender baked fruit—but none of the fussy technique. With galettes, you don’t have to worry about any crimping, latticework, or blind baking. Sometimes, it's okay to take the easy road. This classic apple galette is one of our favorite examples. Warm, comforting, and bursting with sweet, spiced flavor, it’s everything you love about apple pie with a fraction of the effort.

What People Are Saying:“I've already made this twice. Really really nice recipe. So fast and simple, not too sweet and not at all goopy. This will be my go-to filling for apple galettes from now on.” - PurpleRing.

It has been revealed that first, combine the apples, brown sugar, lemon juice, cinnamon, and salt in a large bowl. Then, preheat the oven to 400° and prepare a baking sheet by lining it with parchment paper. Coat a clean surface with a dusting of flour, then roll the chilled pie dough into a 12” circle that is about ⅛” thick. Transfer the dough to the baking sheet.

Industry observers note that arrange the apple slices on top of the dough in alternating rows, leaving about a 1 ½” border around the edge. Then, fold the dough edge nearest to you toward the center and rotate the baking sheet, repeating this step until all 4 edges of the dough are folded in toward the fruit.

Brush the egg wash over the crust and sprinkle demerara sugar over the top. Then place the galette into the oven to bake for 40 to 45 minutes until the crust is golden brown and the fruit is fragrant and tender. Remove the galette from the oven and transfer it to a cooling rack to cool completely before slicing and serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

A galette is essentially an open-faced pie. Thinly sliced apples are tossed in cinnamon and sugar and layered on top of a single sheet of pie crust. The crust is folded over the apples in a rough circle and baked until the crust is flaky. Apple pie has a top and bottom crust and is usually formed in a pie dish. The extra crust and overall shape are the only real differences, and for the apple obsessed, galettes provide the perfect ratio of crust to filling.

It has been revealed that anything you'd serve with an apple pie would work here as well. That means your favorite ice cream, frozen yogurt, caramel sauce, or candied nuts would be great galette sidekicks.

Any leftover galette can be stored for up to 4 days in the refrigerator.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that this beloved American fast-food chain is known for its ButterBurgers and frozen custard. Can you guess?

In a recent development, pop the cheese curds, Wisconsin! Forbes just released its first-ever America’s Favorite Restaurants list, and the No. 1 spot didn’t go to Chick-fil-A, McDonald’s or any coastal cult favorite (lookin’ at you, In-N-Out). It went to Culver’s.

To build the ranking, Forbes partnered with data and insights manufacturer HundredX to poll more than 100,000 Americans about 100 restaurants, from sit-down chains and fast-food spots to coffee shops that serve food. The survey considered eight categories: taste, price, food quality, menu, value, atmosphere, cleanliness and speed.

The Midwestern chain known for its ButterBurgers, frozen custard, crinkle-cut fries and breaded cheese curds scored extra well in taste and food quality. Honestly, anyone who’s ended a long day with a Concrete Mixer already knew that.

According to recent reports, we’ll admit to some hometown pride here. Taste of Home is based in Wisconsin too, so watching a homegrown favorite take it all feels a little like seeing your cousin’s pie win the county fair.

It has been revealed that culver’s was founded in 1984 in Sauk City, Wisconsin—about 100 miles from Taste of Home HQ. Today the tech giant is based down the road in Prairie du Sac and has more than 1,000 locations in 26 states. Almost all of them are owned by local franchisees.

In-N-Out Burger came in second, earning strong marks in the menu, price and value categories. Forbes noted that both the No. 1 and No. 2 spots have something in common: They’re burger joints.

Texas-based iced tea chain HTeaO landed in third place, Texas Roadhouse took fourth, and Chick-fil-A rounded out the top five.

In a recent development, the biggest downside for burger fans is that Culver’s isn’t in every state yet. But if you’re planning a holiday road trip, it could be worth checking whether there’s a Culver’s along the way. A ButterBurger and a scoop of the Flavor of the Day make a detour worth every mile. And if there’s not one nearby, these Culver’s copycats will do the trick.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a latest paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as âdynamic fibrils.â They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sunâs outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.

The key to understanding this discrepancy, as weâve said before, is energy transfer. How does the pathway work for energy to come from the Sunâs interior to its upper atmosphere? At this point, the accepted answer seems to be through massive magnetic fields pushing plasma outwards and heating it intensely, but the nuances of the exact mechanism remain hazy.

Recent findings suggest that dynamic fibrils are one such potential mechanism. They are rhythmic jets erupting from the outer haloâknown as the penumbraâsurrounding a sunspot. But up until now we have had difficulty tracking where exactly they go, largely because the Sun is so bright it's hard to isolate individual tendrils from the overall burning mass of plasma.

Fraser attempts to answer why the Sun's corona is hotter than its surface.

Recent findings suggest that to do so, Guotang Wu and Xiaoli Yan of the Yunnan Observatories at the Chinese Academy of Sciences combined data sources. They used the Latest Vacuum Solar Telescope, located in southwestern China, to monitor a sunspot in an active region of the Sun known as NOAA 13182. Crucially, they did so for just over an hour on January 10th, 2023, and took snapshots of the chromosphere â the middle layer between the Sunâs surface and its outer atmosphere â every 45 seconds. They then combined these ground observations with data from Chinaâs CHASE solar satellite and NASAâs Solar Dynamics Observatory, providing a multi-layered and multi-spectral view of this active sunspot.

Over that hour of observations, they catalogued 176 individual dynamic fibrils â jets of plasma that rise off the surface and into the Sunâs atmosphere. On average, they do so at a speed of 16 km/s, faster than the speed of sound in the surrounding plasma medium of the chromosphere. But eventually they slow down, falling back to the surface after an average lifespan of about 4.5 minutes. Even during that time, they manage to stretch on average 1,130 kilometers â roughly the distance from Newly introduced York to Chicago.

Industry observers note that so where do those jets come from in the first place? Sunspots are already famous for creating features known as ârunning penumbral wavesâ of compressed gas that move across the halo surrounding the sunspotâs core. According to math described in the paper, the rhythmic pulsing of the fibrils almost matches the five-minute cadence of the running penumbral waves in the sunspot. This, in turn, points to another underlying phenomena â magnetoacoustic waves.

Fraser talks about the highest resolution image ever taken of the Sun.

Recent findings suggest that under the surface of the Sun, hot convection cells of plasma constantly vibrate features known as âmagnetic flux tubesâ, creating low-frequency sound waves that leak upwards into the chromosphere. As the gas they are traversing gets thinner and thinner, they grow steeper and stronger until they âbreakâ in a similar manner to waves on a beach. However, these breaking waves are not like those of water â each breaking wave is accompanied by a miniature sonic boom known as a magnetoacoustic shock. These push the plasma residing in the chromosphere where they break, pushing chromospheric plasma upward to form dynamic fibrils.

Sources indicate that buried in the data there was a clear pattern of how much the orientation of these magnetic fields matters for the creation of fibrils. When the magnetic field lines point straight up, the plasma jets experience stronger deceleration and pulse at shorter intervals. Whereas when the fields lean more horizontally across the Sunâs surface, the fibrils decelerate more gently and pulse over longer periods. This confirmed a long-standing theory about how magnetic tilt affects solar sound waves.

According to recent reports, to tie all this back to the original theme â extreme coronal heating â observations from SDO revealed corresponding signatures in gas heated to hundreds of thousands or even millions of degrees. So, the plasma pushed up by those shockwaves doesnât just appear to fizzle out - it directly transfers energy into the corona itself, which aligns with what many of the recent papers on this topic have been proving in various ways.

But weâre still not 100% sure of some of the nuances of how this complex magnetic dance actually works. That might have to wait for even bigger ground-based telescopes such as the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, which can resolve the magnetic threads inside these massive jets. But until then, we have an even clearer picture of how an acoustic hum plays a role in stoking the inferno of the Sunâs outer atmosphere.

It’s never too early to get a head start on holiday gifting. After all, getting your shopping done now means you can focus on the notable things once the holidays actually roll around—you know, like spending time with family, cooking a festive feast, and enjoying plenty of mulled cider and wine. If you’re in need of gifts for the food people in your life, look no further. These are the 57 gifts we’re planning to give (or hoping to receive) this year.

A handmade mug is a little luxury they’ll use every day (and think of you when they do!). Tailor your pick to your giftee’s caffeine preferences to make it feel more personal: opt for an oversized mug for the friend who needs drip coffee on an IV, or a more petite cup for the cappuccino drinker.

I recently added these elegant tumblers to my collection thinking they’d be great for dinner parties, and they are—but they’ve also become my upcoming favorite everyday water and iced latte glasses, because while they’re beautiful, they feel sturdy enough for daily use. They bring a smile to my face every time I use them, which is exactly what a great gift should do, isn’t it?

Industry observers note that an olive oil can is the kind of thing that’s meant to live on your counter, so why not upgrade to a beautiful one? This sleek stainless-steel model from Seattle-based design studio Holcomb has been in my gifting rotation since it was released. It goes with multiple different home aesthetics and looks equally at home by the stove as it does on a dinner party table.

It has been revealed that give the designated host friend a set of whimsical spiral-tipped serving utensils to use at their next dinner party. And don’t worry, they’re dishwasher-safe.

Buttered toast is a perfect food, in my opinion, and anyone that agrees will adore this handblown glass butter keeper from East Fork. Its design ensures your butter can be kept at room temperature for weeks without spoiling, which means it’ll stay perfectly spreadable and ready to be swiped across whatever carbs you choose.

Any friend who cooks will appreciate receiving this set of ramekins from cult-favorite pottery brand East Fork. At four ounces, they’re a versatile size that works for equally as well for portioning mise en place as it does for serving condiments or sauces.

Sources indicate that this stylish pepper grinder looks incredibly cool, but it’s also made with function in mind. That swanky-looking handle? It’s designed to be ergonomic, able to be held and twisted in myriad ways depending on what’s most comfortable for the user. This gift set pairs the grinder with Piper’s 50-50 blend of black and red peppercorns, portioned into four individual packets to ensure the spices stay fresh.

Sidekick End Grain Cutting Board.

These stunning wood cutting boards are truly heirloom-worthy, handcrafted by expert woodworkers from sturdy hardwood. They’re versatile pieces that are durable enough to be your everyday chopping boards and beautiful enough to serve as serving vessels for cheese and charcuterie.

In a recent development, you can’t go wrong with a beautiful vase, especially if you fill that vase with a bouquet of fresh flowers. This colorful glass number is sure to earn your giftee compliments, and I love that it’s hand-blown, which means every piece is one-of-a-kind.

Recent findings suggest that you never know when you need a large bowl until you find yourself in need of a large bowl. Any person who likes to host should have a few attractive options on hand, and a splatter enamelware bowl is a pretty timeless choice.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Industry observers note that testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

Recent findings suggest that the bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

Get the friend who nerds out on coffee roasting and fermentation processes a subscription to Podium Coffee Club’s Platinum tier, which sources its monthly beans from award-winning roasters across the country. The Platinum tier is focused on rare coffee varietals made using experimental techniques, so it’s perfect for someone who likes an expressive, unique roast.

This gift set brings a taste of Richard Christiansen’s Flamingo Estate to your pantry. It’s full of high-quality products you’ll actually use—no weird spice blends or waxy chocolates here.

According to recent reports, for the friend who would gladly eat tinned fish for dinner every night, I suggest this 10-pack of greatest hits from Fishwife. It’s got a little bit of everything, from the brand’s smoked salmon collab with Fly By Jing to the fan-favorite Smoked Rainbow Trout with Chimichurri, plus limited edition Little Sardines, which are available only as a part of holiday sets.

According to recent reports, we all know someone who finishes every dish with flaky salt. In a recent development, diaspora Spice Co. spices are nothing like the bottles you'd find at the grocery store. Do a side by side smell test and the difference will be obvious to you. Balsamic Vinegar of Modena & White Condiment Set.

Tawashi Little Fish Dishcloths, Set of 2.

This tortoise-handled bottle opener from Parisian flatware brand Sabre makes for a handsome host gift, especially when paired with a bottle of your favorite pét-nat or non-alc apéritif.

Million-Dollar Mac & Cheese

📅 13 Nov 2024 | ⏱️ 2 min read (465 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my opinion, mac & cheese is a must-have on any holiday table.
  • Sources indicate that the cheeses:Most of the great mac & cheeses I’ve ever eaten contain three distinct cheeses: a base melting cheese, a tangy cheese with some character, and a sharper accent cheese.
  • It has been revealed that the combination of these three cheeses is worth that million-dollar label, so even if you don’t typically buy these cheeses, I urge you to seek them out for this mac.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my opinion, mac & cheese is a must-have on any holiday table. If you’re looking to take the classic from good to million-dollar-price-tag-worthy, then this is the recipe for you. My million-dollar mac & cheese is what happens when you decide to take basic mac & cheese on a shopping spree to the fanciest cheese shop you know and shower it with gold leaf. Showcasing a trifecta of bougie (and delicious) cheeses and a crispy, crunchy panko topping, this irresistible comfort food will take center stage on any table it hits.

Sources indicate that the cheeses:Most of the great mac & cheeses I’ve ever eaten contain three distinct cheeses: a base melting cheese, a tangy cheese with some character, and a sharper accent cheese. For this million-dollar mac, I chose Pecorino Romano as my accent, but went slightly rogue with the other two and paired fontina and French raclette, which both melt well and have quite a bit of funk. French raclette is particularly great for a mac & cheese sauce since it becomes almost fondue-like when melted, giving you cheese pulls beyond your wildest dreams.

It has been revealed that the combination of these three cheeses is worth that million-dollar label, so even if you don’t typically buy these cheeses, I urge you to seek them out for this mac. That said, if you absolutely can’t find them, you could try combining comté and Camembert or Gruyère and brie with the Pecorino to give you a similar result.

Industry observers note that the crispy topping:With a dish as rich and creamy as this mac & cheese, a crispy, crunchy topping is key. Pre-toasting the panko in butter on the stove ensures a truly golden-brown, delicious topping, without the nail-biting broiler-watching session. Using a higher butter-fat European-style butter here (as well as in the sauce) brings additional richness, ensuring this million-dollar mac is as decadent as it should be. In testing, I found that the breadcrumbs on top of the mac didn’t brown much more when they were on top of the mac in the oven, but if you’re concerned about them getting too dark, you can always lightly tent the pan with foil.

Industry observers note that the gold leaf topping is a fun way to cue the whole “million-dollar” thing, but it’s totally not necessary. Use it if you want, but don’t feel obligated!

Industry observers note that storage:Any leftover mac & cheese can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave, covered, in 30-second bursts until warmed through or, if you have enough, in the oven in a covered ceramic dish.

  • âThe system should not exist.â - Professor Patrick Dufour, UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes astronomers search for one thing and find something completely different. There are many examples of that, from the Cosmic Microwave Background to Pulsars to Gamma-Ray Bursts. The same thing happened recently to researchers who were hunting for exoplanets. Instead of distant planets orbiting a distant star, they found an unusual triple star system in our stellar neighbourhood.

Their unexpected discovery is presented in a paper titled "WelopÅâai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. An international team of researchers made the discovery, and the lead author is Ãtienne Artigau. Artigau is from the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

âThe system should not exist.â - Professor Patrick Dufour, UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

In a recent development, âWe were actually looking for planets,â lead author Artigau remarked in a press release. âInstead, we found something much more surprising.â.

IREx is the group behind Canada's contribution to the JWST, the FGS/NIRISS instrument. IREx's other instrumentation projects include the SPIRou and NIRPS high-precision infrared spectrographs, installed in Hawaiâi and Chile respectively, and the GPI imager on the Gemini-South telescope. This discovery began with the SPIRou (SpectroPolarimeter Infrared) instrument, which uses the radial velocity method to detect exoplanets tugging on their stars.

But in this case, instead of finding an exoplanet tugging on a star, they found another star tugging on a star.

According to recent reports, "Serendipity has long played a key role in astronomy, offering insights into fresh phenomena," the researchers point out. "We report the serendipitous discovery of a white dwarf companion to the M4 V dwarf WelopÅâai Aa (IRAS 21500+5903) during a radial-velocity search for exoplanets with SPIRou," the authors write in their paper. "The system is located at 8.46 pc and forms a hierarchical triple with a more distant white dwarf, which has no known analogue within 30 pc.".

Astronomers have watched the M dwarf, named IRAS 21500+5903 (also called TYC 3980-1081-1 A), and known about its unusual radial velocity (RV) signal since 2019. In this work, the researchers used SPIRou to gather almost five years of RV data on the red dwarf. That data revealed that the RV signal had a large amplitude, which was inconsistent with an exoplanet signal. Exoplanets produce small wobbles as they tug on their stars.

"The mid-M dwarf demonstrated a near-constant acceleration of approximately 5 m sâ1 dâ1 (â¼1800 m sâ1 yrâ1), a level inconsistent with a planetary companion: on a few-year orbit around a 0.42 Mâ star, even a Jupiter-mass planet would induce an acceleration of at most â¼40â130 m sâ1 yrâ1," the authors write.

That's math-speak for saying that the RV signal is up to 45 times stronger than a planet the mass of Jupiter could produce.

This figure highlights the RV curve of WelopÅâai Aa from SPIRou observations spanning 4.8 yr, with the best-fit Keplerian model overplotted. The inset shows one week of observations, and shows how precise the measurements were. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321.

Astronomers already knew that the M dwarf had a binary companion. It's a white dwarf, the massive dead core of a star that was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But that star is too far away to be responsible for the RV signal. Instead, another massive white dwarf was most likely close to the M dwarf.

According to recent reports, âThe objectâs unusual combination of high mass and dim light left only one plausible explanation: it was the remains of a dead star,â said co-author Charles-Antoine Parent, a Mastersâ student at the University of Montreal. âThe most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldnât be ruled out.â.

To narrow it down, the researchers turned to the Gemini North Telescope and its âAlopeke instument. âAlopeke is a high-resolution imager that can eliminate distortion caused by Earth's atmosphere.

According to recent reports, âAlopeke revealed the nature of the third star in the system, showing that it was a second white dwarf that forms an inner pair. "This inner pair lies at a projected separation of 123.9 au (Pâ>â1000 yr) from a previously known white dwarf," the authors write.

These panels show Alopeke observations in three different epochs, with yellow arrows showing the upcoming white dwarf's position in December 2023 and 2024. It's more visible in some channels than others. The M dwarf is the central bright spot or region, it's shape distorted in the effort to highlight the white dwarf. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321.

Determining the mass of a solitary white dwarf is challenging. There are billions of them in the galaxy, but precise mass measurements of them are very rare. Only a handful of masses have been determined for nearby white dwarfs. Determining their masses in binary stars is easier, and because the latest white dwarf interacts gravitationally with the red dwarf, the researchers could determine its mass dynamically, rather then depending on its brightness or its spectrum.

According to recent reports, they found that the new white dwarf companion has about 0.62 solar masses. "The dynamically determined mass of the inner white dwarf is one of only a handful of such measurements for white dwarfs within 20 pc, and the most precise, at the sub-percent (0.7%) level," the researchers explain.

The system has been named WelopÅâai, a Hawaiian word that combines welo (an inherited or family trait) and pÅâai (an orbit or encircling path), together evoking a âpath of family traits.â The primary red dwarf is designated WelopÅâai Aa, its newly discovered close white dwarf partner is WelopÅâai Ab, and the outer white dwarf is WelopÅâai B.

This graphic demonstrates observations of the WelopÅÊ»ai triple-star system, located only 28 light-years from Earth. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: WelopÅÊ»ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and WelopÅÊ»ai B, a second white dwarf much farther away. The image on the right is a close-up view of the inner pair, and it shows the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) that was detected with the Gemini North telescopeâs âAlopeke instrument. The overlaid curves illustrate the starsâ orbital paths. Image Credit: Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST (left); International Gemini Observatory/NSF.

This system is very unusual, and rare. By determining its mass so accurately, the discovery will inform models of stellar evolution, something astrophysicists are always keen to improve.

âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises.â - Ãtienne Artigau, IREx, University of Montreal.

The newly introduced white dwarf was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But since it's so close to the red dwarf, the pair most likely interacted gravitationally at earlier stages of the white dwarf's evolution. It's possible that the two were inside a common envelope at one point, a situation where an envelope of gas surrounds both stars. That often forces the stars to spiral inward and merge. That should have destroyed WelopÅÊ»ai A, the red dwarf. But it appears to be intact, which is surprising. Somehow it survived that disruptive, turbulent scenario and follows a stable orbit.

Recent findings suggest that âThe system should not exist,â states Prof. Patrick Dufour, white dwarf specialist at UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al and co-author of the study. âWe have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.â.

Recent findings suggest that there are still some unexplained things about this system. The red dwarf is between 9 and 11 billion years old, yet is suprisingly metal-rich. Stars this old aren't expected to have such high metallicity. "Reproducing the metallicity would require the M dwarf to have captured roughly two-thirds of the metals, and almost none of the hydrogen or helium, ejected by the inner WDâs progenitor," the authors write, and there's no known mechanism that could do this.

"These puzzles, together with the still-open question of how the inner binary avoided a classical common-envelope in-spiral, identify WelopÅâai as a valuable benchmark for future work on binary-star pollution and tidal evolution," the authors write.

In a recent development, âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,â remarked Artigau. âEven when weâre searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us!â.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there are certain foods that we wish we could package up and save forever, and tomatoes are at the top of that list. Canning is an excellent way to hold onto the fleeting abundance of summer, when these versatile fruits are at their ripest, juiciest, and most flavorful. Canning may never be able to re-create the feeling of picking a plump, juicy tomato fresh from the vine and slicing it while it’s still warm from the sun, but in the depths of winter, we’ll take what we can get. Whether they are using diced, puréed, crushed, or whole canned tomatoes, these recipes make the most of the ingredient, extending its life well beyond the growing season.

Recent findings suggest that this classic sauce from Bolognese cooking teachers Margherita and Valeria Simili combines ground beef with prosciutto, chicken livers, milk, and tomato purée. The slow-simmered sauce is a natural partner for serving over pasta or as a hearty filling for lasagna. Get the recipe >.

Recent findings suggest that stalks of crisp celery are cut into bite-size pieces and slowly braised with tomatoes, onion, prosciutto, and olive oil until tender. This simple Italian preparation transforms a vegetable that’s often an afterthought into a comforting side dish. Get the recipe >.

Industry observers note that agrodolce, or “sour and sweet” in Italian, is a classic Sicilian sauce, here paired with tender steamed broccoli. Red wine, canned tomatoes, vinegar, raisins, and black olives give the sauce its characteristic sweet-tart and slightly salty balance, while toasted pine nuts add a little crunch. Get the recipe >.

In this simple recipe, beef short ribs slowly braise with red wine, garlic, onion, and canned tomatoes until the meat is fall-apart tender. It’s a hearty, straightforward one-pot meal that makes especially good use of pantry staples. Get the recipe >.

This stuffed pasta with ridged edges from celebrated Los Angeles chef Evan Funke pairs a filling of ricotta and greens with a humble lightly cooked tomato sauce. Get the recipe >.

Industry observers note that this classic Sicilian dish balances tender fried eggplant with caramelized onions, golden raisins, olives, capers, and a sweet-tart tomato sauce. An unexpected addition of unsweetened chocolate brings a subtle bitterness that rounds out the sweet and savory flavors. Get the recipe >.

While not the pizza that many people think of, this beloved Rhode Island specialty features thick, airy rectangles of focaccia-like dough topped with a simple tomato sauce. Traditionally served at room temperature, they’re a fixture at bakeries, parties, and family gatherings. Get the recipe >.

In a recent development, lamb, torn pita, and herbs are formed into tender rounds and simmered in a spicy tomato sauce, then finished with a cool, lemony aioli. The dish can be prepared ahead and reheated before serving, with the greens and sauce added at the last minute. Get the recipe >.

According to recent reports, A tomato-packed broth made with topneck clams and salt pork provides the foundation for this hearty soup. The mixture is chilled overnight, giving the flavors time to meld before being finished with bacon, onion, celery, garlic, and fresh herbs. Get the recipe >.

Industry observers note that roasted pumpkin, winter squash, sweet potato, and bell pepper are folded into a tomato-based sauce spiced with cumin, coriander, and harissa. Chickpeas and dried apricots make the stew hearty and subtly sweet, while bulgur mixed with dried cherries and raisins makes for a flavorful, filling base. Get the recipe >.

These crisp, golden fritters bring together tender Sea Island red peas, Carolina Gold rice, and collard greens in a nod to the flavors of South Carolina’s Lowcountry. The accompanying sauce simmers canned tomatoes with brown sugar, cider vinegar, and smoked paprika, creating a bright, tangy dip with just a hint of sweetness and smoke. Get the recipe >.

Industry observers note that this Sicilian baked pasta layers ring-shaped noodles with a tomato-rich ragù of beef, pork, and peas, plus fried eggplant, hard-boiled eggs, ham, and cheese. It’s the kind of deeply layered, all-in-one dish that makes for the perfect centerpiece when cooking for a crowd. Get the recipe >.

This Roman classic gets its character from slow-braised oxtail and an unusually simple combination of tomatoes and celery, with no garlic or onions. The sauce is even better made a day or two ahead, giving the flavors time to deepen before it’s tossed with the cooked pasta. Get the recipe >.

It has been revealed that creamy polenta provides the filling backbone of this dish, while sausage stewed in marinara sauce brings a rich, savory depth. Finished with grated Pecorino Romano, it’s a classic Italian comfort food that’s hearty, satisfying, and perfect for a cozy dinner. Get the recipe >.

In a recent development, this cultural mash-up pairs chewy udon noodles with a deeply savory tomato sauce spiked with guanciale, white miso, chile, and Pecorino Romano. The sauce starts with canned San Marzano tomatoes, which simmer with garlic and onion until thick and rich. Get the recipe >.

It has been revealed that this southern Italian dish from famed cookbook author Marcella Hazan pairs seared lamb chops with a simple skillet sauce of canned San Marzano tomatoes, sweet red peppers, green olives, onion, and parsley. The chops finish in the sauce, picking up its savory, briny flavor. Get the recipe >.

Industry observers note that fresh chiles are cooked alongside onions, garlic, and spices, providing an aromatic base for the sauce of crushed tomatoes. Eggs provide a hit of protein and a richness to counteract the sauce’s heat and acidity, while a sprinkling of feta cheese and chopped parsley add a touch of saltiness and verdant freshness. Get the recipe >.

According to recent reports, A year-round take on a classic Italian summer salad, this version uses canned tomatoes to soak into dry country bread, along with roasted fennel, fresh mozzarella, peppery arugula, and bitter radicchio. Get the recipe >.

Sources indicate that marcella Hazan’s classic tomato sauce proves that great Italian cooking doesn’t need to be complicated. Canned tomatoes simmer gently with butter and onion, creating a rich, silky sauce with remarkable depth and a subtle sweetness. The result is a simple sauce that lets the quality of its few ingredients shine. Get the recipe >.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, by the 1970s, scientists largely accepted the theory that the Universe was permeated by a dark, invisible mass that prevented galaxies from flying apart. While scientists had speculated about the existence of "Dark Matter" for years, it was the work of Vera C. Rubin that made it official. By the 1990s, deep field observations made by the venerable Hubble Space Telescope led scientists to theorize that there was a powerful cosmic force driving expansion, what would come to be known as "Dark Energy.".

Sources indicate that these two theories have become part of the predominantly accepted model of the Universe, known as the Lambda Cold Dark Matter (ÎCDM) model. However, alternative theories, like the Covarying Coupling Constants plus Tired Light (CCC+TL), still endure. Between 2025 and 2026, researchers at the University of Ottawa (go GeeGees!) tested the CCC+TL model against a range of important astronomical observations. The model passed these tests, challenging what we think we know about the Universe.

The research was conducted by Rajendra Gupta, an Adjunct Professor in uOttawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras. As they described, they tested the CCC+TL model against the predicted abundance of certain elements (hydrogen, helium, and other light elements) shortly after the Massive Bang, using cosmic-chronometer measurements. Their results are detailed in a paper published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

It has been revealed that the cosmic Dark Ages refer to the first one billion years after the Substantial Bang and before the formation of the first stars and galaxies. Credit: NASA.

While scientists have observed considerable indirect evidence for Dark Matter and Dark Energy (DM and DE), no direct detections have been made, despite decades of research. In addition, the ÎCDM model has faced challenges in recent years, as observations by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) revealed an abundance of mature galaxies in the early Universe. This has led to renewed interest in alternative theories such as Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) and CCC+TL.

In a recent development, the latter model suggests that what is usually attributed to DM and DE could instead come from evolving fundamental constants that govern how forces and particles interact. In particular, CCC+TL changes Einstein's field equations for General Relativity (which describes gravity) and the FriedmannâLemaÃ®tre (FL) equations that describe cosmic expansion (aka. the Hubble-LemaÃ®tre Constant). Moreover, it uses the ages of galaxies to estimate how fast the Universe has expanded over time. As Gupta summarized:.

Industry observers note that most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations. A upcoming model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.

It has been revealed that for their simulations, Gupta and Samaras couldn't simply modify standard computer models; they had to develop CCC+TL-compliant equations and code. As they describe in their paper, the model's results agreed with several major observations. They further applied the model to the 175 galaxies in the SPARC database and found that it reproduced their rotational curves without dark matter. They also applied it to the famous Bullet Cluster, a pair of merging galaxy clusters from which Rubin derived much of the evidence for DM.

In this case, the extra gravitational effect predicted by the CCC+TL model was consistent with observations of the clusters, which the researchers consider an early proof of concept. Alongside Utkarsh Kumar, a postdoctoral researcher in observational cosmology at uOttawa, Gupta and Samara applied the model to observations of time dilation in supernovae. Their results are described in a separate study that is still pending review. In another study, Gupta proposes that observations attributed to DM and DE likely originated from covarying coupling constants.

Age comparison against redshift in CCC+TL and ÎCDM models. Credit: uOttawa/Gupta et al. (2026).

In a recent development, in the standard model, the Universe was only about 300 million years old when the first stars and galaxies began forming, a period known as Cosmic Dawn. Under CCC+TL, the Universe would have been about 4.6 billion years old during this period, which would be long enough for the early galaxies observed by Webb to have formed and matured. In summary, the CCC+TL model suggests that we live in a Universe much older than 13.8 billion years, placing its age at around 26.7 billion years.

Industry observers note that upcoming observations will offer additional opportunities to test this new model. For example, there's the General Observations (GO) GO 3293 GLIMPSE program, or the Gravitational Lensing and NIRCam IMaging Program to probe Early galaxy formation and Sources of reionization. This ultra-deep observation program will use the JWST's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) and gravitational lensing from the Abell S1063 galaxy cluster to study early galaxy formation and cosmic reionization. Said Gupta:.

Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies. We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached. The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ÎCDM limits.

Further Reading: University of Ottawa.

It has been revealed that if you’re latest to Nespresso, the main thing you need to know is that there are two lines of machines: The Original Line (often written as OriginalLine) and the Vertuo Line (sometimes written as Verutoline). You need, expectedly, Original capsules for Original machines and Vertuo capsules for Vertuo machines. I've broken down the differences between the lines below, and the defining details about specific models in each line that are on sale right now. And be sure to bookmark this story because we’ll revision it with more Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals on Nespresso coffee makers and espresso machines as they happen.

Introduced in 2014, Nespresso’s Vertuoline modernized the brand’s original pressure brew method and marked the true beginning of Nespresso espresso and coffee machines. Most Vertuo machines feature just one button and brew both coffee and espresso-style shots using a centrifugal method. Once you choose your preferred pod based on style, roast, and cup size, the machine takes care of the rest. That’s because the rim of every dome-shaped Vertuo capsule features a barcode that tells the Nespresso Vertuo machine how much water and what extraction speed to use for each pod—and can brew everything from a single and double espresso shot to a 14-ounce cup of coffee. Some Vertuo machines can even fill an 18-ounce carafe from a single coffee pod.

The very first Vertuo machine released more than a decade ago is still kicking, and it's one of the best values you can get.

Enabled with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, the Nespresso Vertuo Next can brew 18 ounces of coffee from a single pod. If you’re intrigued by the tech or pod yield, it’s worth a try—especially considering Nespresso’s 30-day return policy, warranty, and reputation for maintenance and machine repairs.

Vertuo Next Coffee with Aeroccino Milk Frother.

In a recent development, modeled on the Vertuo Next, this compact cutie is one of the newer Vertuo machines. It’s perfect for someone who’s short on space but still wants the convenience of the Vertuoline. The Pop Plus machines have slightly bigger water reservoirs than the Pop models, and they can hold more used capsules, but all of the machines have small-kitchen-friendly footprints.

Nespresso Vertuo Pop + Aeroccino Milk Frother.

Recent findings suggest that released earlier this year, the Vertuo Up is Nespresso's newest machine, and brews the one-touch Vertuo pods. This compact machine heats up in just three seconds (which, is really, really, ridiculously fast for any coffee maker to heat water) and depending on the specific model you get, it can brew six or seven different cup sizes, ranging from a single shot of espresso to a full carafe from a single Vertuo pod. Like the Next and Pop machines, the Vertuo Up is Wi-Fi enabled and you can use the companion app for maintenance alerts and to customize how the machine brews your favorite pods, if you'd like tweaks to the pod-specific presets.

The Vertuo Creatista is the first machine in the Vertuo line with a built-in steam wand. It’s not quite a one-touch cappuccino machine because brewing espresso from a pod and steaming the milk are two separate processes. But if you want the look of a real espresso machine (well, if you don’t look too closely) with the convenience of Nespresso Vertuo capsules, the Vertuo Creatista is a great option. This is the machine that I’ve been using at home for years and it works sort of like a super-automatic espresso machine.

  • It has been revealed that in the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks.
  • Now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party.

It has been revealed that in the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Industry observers note that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development.

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for Fresh Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Recent findings suggest that as the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content.

In a recent development, I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer.

There are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor.

Industry observers note that several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director.

#88754. Breaking: Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1292 w)

Breaking: Complex Life on Earth May Not Have Appeared Without Tall Mountains

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the more scientists learn about Earth, the more habitability appears to involve an almost kaleidoscopic array of variables and interactions.
  • It has been revealed that new research suggests that another factor may come into play: mountains.
  • Sources indicate that their main claim is that mountains are critical because they increase the surface area exposed to weathering, and that makes notable chemicals and nutrients available, as well as changing the chemistry of the oceans and the atmosphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the more scientists learn about Earth, the more habitability appears to involve an almost kaleidoscopic array of variables and interactions. Though our current search for potentially habitable worlds is mostly restricted to finding rocky planets with liquid water and atmospheres, it will have to advance well beyond that to bear fruit. Things like exoplanet plate tectonics to keep climates moderate, and stars with long, stable lifetimes that let life fluorish and evolve are factors in habitability.

It has been revealed that new research suggests that another factor may come into play: mountains. The research is titled "Raising mountains for a habitable Earth," and it's published in Science Advances. The lead author is Dr. Matthijs Smit of the University of British Columbiaâs Department of Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences.

Sources indicate that their main claim is that mountains are critical because they increase the surface area exposed to weathering, and that makes notable chemicals and nutrients available, as well as changing the chemistry of the oceans and the atmosphere. That, in turn, led to the eventual appearance of complex life.

"The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability," the authors write.

Industry observers note that K2 is the second tallest mountain in the world. The crust underneath it is some of the thickest in the world. Research reveals that in Earth's past, the crust thickened in some places, leading to the growth of very tall mountains. Increased weathering from those mountains preceded the planet's episodes of oxygenation, and researchers hypothesize that episodic spurts of mountain growth enabled Earth's habitability, and the eventual appearance of complex life. Image Credit: By Zacharie Grossen - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/42469860.

According to recent reports, "Continental silicate weathering controls the oceanward flux of carbon and bioactive nutrients that limit marine primary productivity, thus exerting control on atmospheric chemistry, climate, and marine biomass and biodiversity," they explain. "The majority of the global terrigenous runoff derives from mountainous regions.".

The researchers focused on the last three billion years of Earth's history. They examined metamorphic rocks that were pushed deep underground by overlying tectonic plates. When mountains formed where plates collided, the mountains were able to reach much greater heights. That raised nutrient levels in the oceans, which helped photosynthesizing lifeforms oxygenate Earth's atmosphere.

âChanges that occurred deep in the Earth ultimately gave rise to much taller mountains over time, which may have made our planet habitable by providing the nutrients needed for life to form and flourish,â lead author Smit stated. âNutrients such as phosphorous are essential ingredients for life on our planet, but prior to three billion years ago, these elements were locked in the Earthâs crust and the oceans were quite nutrient-starved. All this changed when tall mountains started to develop.â.

In a recent development, the research indicates that two periods of peak metamorphic pressure inside the planet, between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, led to thicker crusts in mountain-forming regions, and that let taller mountains form. The growth of Earth's mountains spiked, and those orogenic growth spurts were synchronous with other important changes on the planet.

Recent findings suggest that âThe first growth spurt may have led to the emergence of land on a large scale for the first time, while the second growth spurt thrust mountain ranges to enormous heights,â remarked co-author Dr. Douwe van Hinsbergen of Utrecht University, The Netherlands. âGiven such profound effects, mountains may well have played a far greater role in the creation of a habitable planet than previously assumed.â.

It has been revealed that earth's atmospheric oxygen rose in distinct periods, and the most well-known and consequential one was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE) from about 2.4 to 2.0 billion years ago. The researchers say that by the time the GOE occurred, Earth's mountains had grown substantially. They rose from near sea-level to about half the height of the modern-day Himalayas. Another distinct period of rising atmospheric oxygen was the Neoproterozoic Oxygen Event (NOE) from around 700 million to 500 million years ago. Mountain growth spiked at that time, too, according to the researchers. Various other atmospheric factors and oceanic factors related to habitability and complex life increased, too.

This figure shows time on the x-axis and more other information throughout. Blue shows how atmospheric O2 pressure rose compared to modern levels, especially during the GOE and the NOE. Purple shows the rise of sulfur isotope diversity, a measure of biological sulfur metabolism over time, and grey shows the percentage of oceanic strontium that comes from continental mountain erosion. Green shows the rise of organisms capable of oxygenic photosynthesis. The snowflake symbols show Earth's main icehouse stages. Image Credit: Smit et al. Science Advances 13 Nov 2026 Vol 12, Issue 46.

Sources indicate that the timing of these spurts of mountain growth coincided with the growth of crustal thickness in mountain belts. In these belts, the thickness of the upper accreted crust grows as plates collide. The first episode increased thickness from 30km to 60 km, and the second episode saw an increase to almost 90 km. âWe suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,â Dr. Smit said. âAs a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.â.

According to recent reports, "Causes for environmental upheaval culminating in the GOE and NOE have been sought in various external forcing mechanisms, such as increased runoff resulting from supercontinent breakup, enhanced weathering of basaltic rocks at low latitude, and a dwindling CO2 (carbon dioxide) flux from arc volcanism," the authors write. While the researchers agree that these are valid hypotheses, they also point out that they're transient. That doesn't match the "irreversible nature of global oxygenation," and other changes. They're also not restricted to periods preceding the GOE and NOE.

The two episodes of crustal thickening and resulting spikes in mountain elevation and erosion are a better fit. "In contrast to all of these processes, the orogenic growth associated with tectonic revolutions R1 and R2 broadly coincide with the major periods of environmental upheaval in terms of their approximate timing, paucity, and irreversibility," the authors write.

According to recent reports, the researchers couldn't measure the height of long-gone mountains, but they were able to determine the density and thickness of ancient crust. Since crustal thickness and density correlate with mountain height, they could calculate the height of ancient mountains.

In a recent development, earth's tallest mountains today, Mount Everest, K2 and Kangchenjunga, are almost certainly some of the tallest ever produced. They approach nine km above sea level, and the crust under them is about 80 km thick. That's twice as thick as other continents. They illustrate how crustal thickness generates tall mountains, and emphasize the hypothesis that mountain growth helped enable Earth's habitability.

Sources indicate that âItâs likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,â mentioned co-author Dr. Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm. âItâs exciting to think that mountain belts were once non-existent and that their development over the past three billion years may have driven the environmental and biological change that shaped our planet.â.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability.
  • The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite all the hype about a fresh space economy, humanity has yet to reap much benefit offered by the prospect of offworld mining, manufacturing, or space tourism.

But historical precedent dictates that ventures into the unknown need to be driven by commerce to achieve profitability. Such was the case five centuries ago, when most of Western Europe was agog over the importation of precious spices from East Asia.

The idea was to circumvent the Silk Road from and drive the spice trade from overland camel caravans to large cargo-holding ships.

For centuries, camels had enabled trickles of spices such as cloves, nutmeg, and ginger to make their way into the kitchens of the high and mighty, be they landed gentry or royalty.

Cloves originally grew in the volcanic soils of only a handful of small islands in the northern Moluccas archipelago, author Lewis Dartnell notes in his 2019 book âOrigins: How the Earth Shaped Human History.â And the nutmeg tree appeared on only nine pinprick-sized islands --- the Bandas-further south, Dartnell writes.

In a recent development, dried nutmeg. Credit: Wikipedia.

But as early as the late 15th century and the Age of Columbus, middlemen had run up the cost of these rare spices to such a degree that Portugal and Spain, in particular, were in competition for a sea route to the Moluccas. That is, the Moluccan archipelago in what is now Indonesia.

The idea was to travel point to point by sea and weed out a multitude of middlemen along the long Silk Road --- mostly stretching overland from the Black Sea and Mediterranean through northern India to China.

Thus, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan had a novel idea.

Magellan, born into a family of minor nobility and modest possessions, had somehow convinced Spainâs King Charles V that it was possible to reach the eastern riches by traveling west, author Romeu Gaspar writes in his 2026 book âThe Revolution of Magellan: How 500-Year-Old Rocket Science Changed the World.â.

And even though Magellan tragically lost his life en route at least a remainder of his crew did circumnavigate the globe. In the process, they forever changed the course of history, commerce, and human exploration.

Dried spices were a lightweight, high-value, reasonably imperishable product with which to stuff a ship's hold on long voyages, John Keay writes in his 2005 book âThe Spice Route: A History.â The profits were huge; in 1515, the return on such cargo docked at Lisbon was 700 per cent, Keay notes.

By 1520, the income from Portugalâs spice trade provided 40 percent of the Crownâs total revenue, Dartnell writes in his book. Spices eventually became so prized that in 1677, the Dutch swapped the island of Manhattan for the nutmeg-rich island of Run Palau, he notes.

A 21st century analogy to such commercial exploration might be if by the end of this century, space entrepreneurs were able to extract and then process rare minerals from the Moon or Mars or even accessible Main Belt asteroids. And then in a cost-efficient manner, reap the profits by bringing them back to Earth. Or at least low-Earth orbit.

Sources indicate that to that end, NASA Apollo 17 astronaut and geologist Harrison Jack Schmitt has long argued for Helium-3 mining on the Moon. But until someone fulfills the economics of making cislunar Space profitable human exploration of our solar system is likely to lag. That's because throughout history, scientific innovation usually goes hand in hand with someone's quest for a large profit margin.

In a recent development, A durable commercial reason for people to work in space could give human space science the transportation and infrastructure it needs, Ret. U.S. Brigadier Gen. Pete Worden, an astrophysicist, chairman of the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, and Laureate Professor at the University of Arizona in Tucson, told me via email.

Within the next fifty years at least, the future of scientific space exploration is arguably best served by robotic means rather than astronauts.

Recent findings suggest that iâd rely heavily on robots for science and give commercial companies a larger role in developing and operating human spaceflight systems, Worden, who directed NASA Ames Research Center from 2006 to 2015, told me via email. NASA should return to its roots in the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) by emphasizing research and technology development that industry and scientists can build on, he states.

Routine human sorties beyond low-earth orbit are key.

If commercial space transportation becomes routine, agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) could support research that uses it, Worden argues.

Meanwhile, we are left with space programs that for decades have been hampered by both politics and economics and as a result, have limped along in fits and starts.

In a recent development, over the past 30 years, NASAâs aims for the Moon and Mars have had to survive changes in administrations, budgets, and priorities, notes Worden. When a program needs agreement from too many people, it becomes harder to take sensible risks, he says.

If humanity can ever succeed in making forays beyond low Earth orbit that are commercially viable in the same way the 16th Century spice trade was profitable, then this latest ocean of space-time could be ours for the taking.
