💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sixty years ago, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies on Gemini XII.
  • Recent findings suggest that sixty years ago this month, Buzz Aldrin opened the hatch of his Gemini spacecraft, looked outside and exclaimed, “Man!
  • Recent findings suggest that near the end of that spacewalk, on November 12, 1966, he mounted a camera on the edge of the hatch, pointed it at himself and took the first selfies ever taken during a spacewalk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sixty years ago, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies on Gemini XII. NASA indicates Gemini photos also helped make the case for satellites like Landsat.

Recent findings suggest that sixty years ago this month, Buzz Aldrin opened the hatch of his Gemini spacecraft, looked outside and exclaimed, “Man! Look at that!”.

Recent findings suggest that near the end of that spacewalk, on November 12, 1966, he mounted a camera on the edge of the hatch, pointed it at himself and took the first selfies ever taken during a spacewalk. NASA notes that it happened decades before the concept even existed.

That flight, Gemini XII, is better known for something else. It finally showed that astronauts could do useful work outside a spacecraft, a skill NASA needed before it could send anyone to the Moon.

And a NASA image article published on November 13 points to a quieter legacy: photos like the ones Aldrin and his commander took from orbit helped inspire the program that led to the Landsat satellites.

Recent findings suggest that aldrin and command pilot James A. Lovell rolled out on November 11, 1966, on a four-day mission. It was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini program, which had to prove the techniques that Apollo would need to land on the Moon.

Those techniques included rendezvous and docking, spacewalking, and showing that spacecraft and astronauts could function for at least eight days, the minimum for a round trip to the Moon.

Spacewalks were the weak spot. Astronauts on the Gemini IX, X and XI missions had run into significant difficulties outside their spacecraft, and NASA looked for better ways to train.

Sources indicate that on September 12, 1966, Aldrin became the first astronaut to train for his spacewalks underwater, using mockups of the Gemini and its target vehicle in a school swimming pool in Owings Mills, Maryland. Neutral buoyancy training, as it is called, is still in use today.

Sources indicate that gemini XII launched about 90 minutes after an uncrewed Agena target vehicle. When the crew’s rendezvous radar proved erratic, Aldrin used backup methods and onboard calculations to guide them in.

He had written his doctoral dissertation on orbital rendezvous. They docked on the third orbit.

A problem with the Agena’s engine stopped a planned boost to a higher orbit. Instead, Mission Control told the crew that a slight change would put them on the path of a solar eclipse the next morning.

On November 12, as they flew over the Galapagos Islands, the nearly total eclipse came into view, and Aldrin took several photographs and a short film clip.

It was the first time a solar eclipse was photographed from Earth orbit, according to NASA. Gemini XII passed within 3.4 miles of the center of the eclipse’s path.

Later that day, Aldrin made his first spacewalk, a “standup” outing in which he stayed in the open hatch. He installed a handrail on the Agena for the next day, photographed stars in ultraviolet light and took his selfies. He spent two hours and 28 minutes outside.

The next day, tied to the spacecraft by a 30-foot umbilical, he moved along the handrail to the Agena and later worked at the back of the Gemini with his feet in restraints called “golden slippers.”.

It has been revealed that he completed 19 tasks in all, reporting no problems with keeping his body in position. At two hours and nine minutes, it was the longest umbilical spacewalk to that time.

Sources indicate that A third standup spacewalk brought his total to a then-record five hours and 48 minutes. Aldrin credited his underwater training and adequate restraint systems for his success.

Spacewalks have come a long way since then: in September 2024, the crew of SpaceX’s Polaris Dawn mission carried out the first civilian spacewalk.

On November 14, 1966, Lovell and Aldrin also photographed the area around the Red Sea and the Nile River valley. NASA featured that image in its November 13 article.

According to the agency, the photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface, and helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program.

According to recent reports, one of the strongest advocates for Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, director of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from 1965 to 1971.

In a 1969 statement, he mentioned the Earth Resources Observation Satellite program he championed, which later paved the way for Landsat, was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.”.

For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have been used to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health and land use. In October, Landsat 9 captured autumn’s colors in the forests around Ripton, Vermont.

Recent findings suggest that lovell and Aldrin splashed down in the Atlantic Ocean on November 15, 1966, only three miles from the planned target. The flight lasted 94 hours and 34 minutes.

In a recent development, gemini flew 10 crewed missions in 20 months, and all of the program’s major objectives were accomplished. Less than three years later, Aldrin walked on the Moon with Apollo 11. The Gemini XII spacecraft is on display at the Adler Planetarium in Chicago.

The information was obtained from NASA’s history of the Gemini XII mission, its account of eclipses seen from space and its image article on Gemini Earth photography.

An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

In a recent development, californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

Recent findings suggest that in 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a substantial, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier states. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

According to recent reports, 1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

It has been revealed that not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” states Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

Sources indicate that but there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto notes. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

Recent findings suggest that as much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

Recent findings suggest that “We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves indicates. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Recent findings suggest that gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

Industry observers note that the havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier claims. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report noted.

Industry observers note that california’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

In a recent development, such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a substantial boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

In a recent development, months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

Recent findings suggest that as prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis notes, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

In a recent development, then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

In a recent development, those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Industry observers note that segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

In a recent development, “Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she indicates. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

According to recent reports, but, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

The 2026 ozone hole grew to more than twice the size of the U.S., but a 1987 treaty kept it from getting even bigger

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole was the seventh largest in 48 years.
  • It has been revealed that this year’s ozone hole over Antarctica grew to cover an area more than twice the size of the United States.
  • Sources indicate that that sounds like bad news, and in part it is.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole was the seventh largest in 48 years. But it would have been bigger without the Montreal Protocol.

It has been revealed that this year’s ozone hole over Antarctica grew to cover an area more than twice the size of the United States. NASA and NOAA scientists say it was the seventh largest in 48 years of monitoring.

Sources indicate that that sounds like bad news, and in part it is. But the same scientists say the ozone layer is still on track to recover later this century, and that the hole would have been even bigger if the world had not cut back on the chemicals that destroy ozone.

Many of those chemicals came from everyday products like refrigerators, air conditioners and building insulation. Some of them are still around, which is one reason the recovery is taking so long.

During the peak ozone depletion season, from September 7 to October 13, the hole covered an average of about 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers), according to NOAA and NASA, which reported the results on November 4.

Industry observers note that it reached its greatest extent for the year on September 18, at 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). That is about 90% as large as the largest ozone hole ever observed, on September 9, 2000.

“The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” remarked Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC), and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the Goddard Space Flight Center.

The word “hole” is not literal. No place is empty of ozone. Scientists use it to describe the area where ozone concentrations drop below 220 Dobson units, a level that had never been observed before 1979.

Industry observers note that the stratospheric ozone layer works as Earth’s sunscreen. It absorbs ultraviolet light, which damages DNA in plants and animals and leads to sunburns and skin cancer in people.

This is not the same as ground-level ozone, an air pollutant that commonly results from human activities and that reached dangerous levels for billions of people in 2026.

Every southern spring, ozone thins over Antarctica. Human-made compounds containing chlorine and bromine rise into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light breaks them down.

The freed chlorine and bromine atoms then interact with cloud particles in the frigid Antarctic stratosphere and destroy ozone.

A ring of seasonal winds called the stratospheric polar vortex keeps that cold air in place. In 2026, the vortex was unusually powerful.

“The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” noted Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory.

That weak wave action kept the strongest winds several degrees of latitude farther from the South Pole, she mentioned, which created a larger area where ozone could be destroyed.

Size is only part of the picture. The 2026 hole was not as deep as the record-breaking holes of 10 or 20 years ago.

NOAA scientists launch balloons carrying instruments called ozonesondes from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory.

According to recent reports, they found that ozone directly overhead reached its lowest value of the year, 105 Dobson units, on October 17. The lowest value ever recorded over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units, in October 2006.

One hundred Dobson units of ozone, compressed at sea level, would make a layer 1 millimeter deep, about as thick as a dime.

“The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” Newman said.

“But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.”.

The ozone hole was first reported in 1985 by British Antarctic Survey scientists, and NASA satellite instruments revealed its continental scale.

Scientists traced the damage to chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, which had been used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays since the 1930s.

That led to the Montreal Protocol in 1987, a treaty in which countries committed to phasing out ozone-depleting substances and replacing them with less harmful alternatives.

According to NOAA and NASA, the controls set by the treaty continue to drive the long-term recovery of the ozone layer.

Since their peak, chlorine levels in the Antarctic stratosphere from ozone-depleting substances have declined by about a third relative to the 1980s, said Stephen Montzka, senior scientist at NOAA’s Global Monitoring Laboratory.

Ozone recovery is also having unexpected effects, like the way it is changing life in Antarctica.

According to recent reports, the ozone hole forms over Antarctica, far from the United States. But the chemicals behind it came from ordinary products, and they do not go away quickly.

Industry observers note that NOAA claims CFCs and similar compounds can linger in the atmosphere, or leak out of old products and landfills, for many decades. As those older compounds break down, scientists estimate that the ozone hole will recover by the 2070s.

In a recent development, that is why the way old appliances are thrown away still matters. Under the Clean Air Act, the Environmental Protection Agency requires refrigerant to be recovered when refrigeration and air conditioning equipment is disposed of, to keep it out of the air.

Household refrigerators and freezers, window air conditioners and car air conditioners usually reach the end of the line with their refrigerant still inside.

In those cases, the EPA says the final person in the disposal chain, such as a scrap metal recycler or a landfill owner, is responsible for making sure the refrigerant is recovered first.

Industry observers note that the EPA also notes that reduced ozone means more UVB radiation reaching the ground. In Antarctica, the amount of UVB measured at the surface can double during the annual ozone hole.

The agency states it is always important to protect yourself from UVB, even without ozone depletion, by wearing hats, sunglasses and sunscreen.

In a recent development, satellites have tracked the ozone layer since 1979. This year, instruments on NASA’s Aura satellite, the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, run jointly by NASA and NOAA, all contributed to the monitoring.

Sources indicate that weather can still make some years worse than others. Year-to-year changes in size and depth are caused by differences in stratospheric temperature and circulation, and colder conditions produce a larger hole, according to NASA’s Earth Observatory.

Without the cuts that began in 1987, this year’s unusually strong vortex would have had more chlorine to work with, and scientists say the hole would have been even larger.

The information was obtained from NOAA, NASA, NASA Earth Observatory and the Environmental Protection Agency’s pages on appliance disposal and the effects of ozone depletion.

The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Big Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator.
  • The term “home generator” can be confusing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly important one.

The term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

Sources indicate that there are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

Once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

The DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

Having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a big boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

Sources indicate that the generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

In a recent development, in addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display shows you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

In a recent development, the only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden.

Technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

In a recent development, its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support revealed its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an matter with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Industry observers note that ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

Whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

While it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

This generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

There are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

There are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (important for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

It’s crucial to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That said, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

It’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

In a recent development, once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review.

Recent findings suggest that battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

During testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

Several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

Meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

One of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

According to recent reports, when AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

This dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

According to recent reports, you can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

Our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

In a recent development, of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review.

In a recent development, pulsar is a relatively newly introduced brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator showed up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

Sources indicate that the generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

According to recent reports, we have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

True whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

It has been revealed that another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

Recent findings suggest that you could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.).

According to recent reports, in addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

According to recent reports, the two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

It has been revealed that if you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, proposal on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

Recent findings suggest that A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It’s also vital to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Recent findings suggest that different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Sources indicate that often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Recent findings suggest that generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other issues in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

So why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

Sources indicate that while often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

Sources indicate that the downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

According to recent reports, they typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

Recent findings suggest that when you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

Sources indicate that this is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

Make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

Never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will swiftly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Industry observers note that set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

Industry observers note that my generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In places where house mice live outdoors for most of the year, the animals often enter homes in autumn and winter as the nights grow colder.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, house mice often enter homes as temperatures drop. Learn how to seal entry points, set traps safely and clean up droppings without risk.

In places where house mice live outdoors for most of the year, the animals often enter homes in autumn and winter as the nights grow colder.

According to recent reports, that pattern is described in a house mouse guide updated in July 2025. Its authors are Niamh Quinn of UC Cooperative Extension and Matt Frye of the Cornell IPM Program.

“House mice can squeeze under gaps ¼ inch tall, and through openings 3/8 inch wide,” the two wrote. Those measurements equal about 6 and 10 millimeters.

The house mouse (Mus musculus) is native to Central Asia. It crossed to North America aboard ships carrying settlers from Europe and elsewhere.

The species lives close to people because they store cereals and grains, the foods it prefers.

An adult weighs about 0.5 ounce (14 grams) and is 5 to 7 inches (13 to 18 centimeters) long, tail included. It can eat up to 20 percent of its body weight a day, taken in roughly 200 small meals each night.

It has been revealed that A house mouse rarely strays more than 30 feet (9 meters) from its nest and its food. It builds that nest in a sheltered spot, using finely shredded paper or other fibrous material.

Industry observers note that where resources stay plentiful and stable, house mice can breed all year. A female may produce five to ten litters in one year, each with about five or six pups.

The young arrive 18 to 21 days after conception and can breed at five to six weeks of age. The usual life span is nine to 12 months.

“If a pen fits under a door, a mouse can enlarge the gap to enter,” Quinn wrote in November 2025. For rats in cities, Quinn put the smallest usable opening at the size of a quarter.

In a recent development, mice climb well and can scale any rough vertical surface. They also run along wire cables and ropes, and can leap as high as 12 inches (30 centimeters) from the floor onto a flat surface.

Entry points listed by Quinn and Frye include cracks in building foundations and the openings around water pipes, vents and utility cables.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises checking inside and outside the home for gaps and holes.

“Exclusion is the most successful and permanent form of house mouse control,” the guide states.

In a recent development, it calls for metal or concrete to seal those cracks and openings. Doors, windows and screens need a tight fit, and door and window edges may need a metal cover to stop gnawing.

Plastic screening, rubber, vinyl, expanding foam and wood are classed as gnawable, and as ineffective plugs for mouse holes.

“Steel wool scouring pads make good temporary plugs but may rust over time,” Quinn and Frye cautioned. The CDC advises steel wool ringed with caulk for small holes, and lath screen or metal, cement, hardware cloth or metal sheeting for larger ones.

Quinn’s article adds door sweeps built to exclude pests, rather than weather strips, and metal mesh over vents.

Ultrasonic devices are of very limited use, because the sound is directional and does not pass behind objects. Some cats and dogs catch mice, but pets seldom keep a rodent population under control.

It has been revealed that for mice already indoors, the California guide favors setting enough traps to keep the trapping period short. It puts the maximum spacing at about 10 feet (3 meters) in areas with mouse activity.

Industry observers note that setting traps in pairs, 1 to 2 inches (2.5 to 5 centimeters) apart, can raise the catch of mice that jump over obstacles. Good spots are behind objects, in dark corners and wherever there is evidence of mice.

Peanut butter is a popular bait because mice find it very attractive, though it can pose allergy risks to some people.

According to recent reports, every rodenticide is toxic to people, pets and wildlife. Poisoned mice often die inside the building being treated, and in that case trapping may be the better approach.

Droppings and gnaw marks can reveal where mice are active. One house mouse leaves approximately 50 to 75 droppings a day, according to University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension.

House mice can carry leptospirosis, salmonella and lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCM), a viral disease. Quinn and Frye cite an estimate that five percent of house mice across the United States carry the LCM virus and can transmit it.

People can catch LCM through exposure to fresh urine, droppings, saliva or nesting material from infected rodents. The most common hantavirus that causes lung disease in the United States comes from another species, the deer mouse.

In a recent development, “Don’t vacuum or sweep rodent urine, droppings, or nesting materials,” the agency’s cleanup instructions warn. That can put tiny droplets carrying viruses into the air.

The steps start with rubber or plastic gloves and a household disinfectant or freshly made bleach solution, left to soak for five minutes. The bleach mix is 1.5 cups (355 milliliters) in 1 gallon (3.8 liters) of water.

The information was obtained from the University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (IPM).

Psoriasis treatment may work better with an over-the-counter supplement

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pantethine, a vitamin B5 relative sold to lower cholesterol, calmed the immune cells behind psoriasis and improved skin in a small trial.
  • Pantethine is a vitamin B5 derivative sold as a dietary supplement.
  • Putting it back calmed the immune cells that drive the disease and eased psoriasis-like inflammation in mice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pantethine, a vitamin B5 relative sold to lower cholesterol, calmed the immune cells behind psoriasis and improved skin in a small trial.

Pantethine is a vitamin B5 derivative sold as a dietary supplement. In a small blood-sample comparison, researchers found lower levels in people with psoriasis than in healthy volunteers.

Putting it back calmed the immune cells that drive the disease and eased psoriasis-like inflammation in mice.

In a small 12-week trial, psoriasis severity scores improved more among patients who took pantethine alongside a prescription ointment than among those who used the ointment alone.

Wei-Na Zhang of the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing led the work with four colleagues, including Cheng-Xin Li of the Chinese PLA General Hospital.

The first authors, Ai-Ping Cao, Jun-Cheng Li and Rui Wang, work at the Beijing laboratory, Fudan University in Shanghai, and the hospital.

Sources indicate that the trial was small and ran at one hospital. The authors wrote that it reveals the approach is feasible, not that the mechanism they found in mice is what helped the patients.

“Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation,” Zhang mentioned.

Psoriasis is an immune disease that happens to show on the skin.

Immune cells called dendritic cells, whose job is to show the rest of the immune system what to attack, get overactive. They set off the inflammation that produces the scaly plaques.

Sources indicate that the team went looking for enzymes that were unusually busy in those cells. In blood and skin samples from patients with psoriasis, lupus and other immune diseases, a family of enzymes called Vanins stood out.

In one set of skin biopsies, from 92 psoriasis patients and 82 healthy people, two of the three Vanin genes were among the most strongly switched on.

Vanins break pantethine down, and one of the products is vitamin B5. In blood from 12 psoriasis patients, pantethine was lower than in 17 healthy people, and mice with psoriasis-like inflammation demonstrated the same shortfall.

The team worked in mice given a cream that triggers psoriasis-like skin inflammation over six days.

Mice whose dendritic cells lacked the main mouse Vanin gene, Vnn3, developed much milder disease, with less skin thickening, lower severity scores and fewer immune cells in the affected patches.

Recent findings suggest that giving ordinary mice a daily injection of pantethine during the six days did the same, and so did a drug called RR6 that blocks Vanin. Both raised pantethine and lowered cholesterol in the blood.

Was it the dendritic cells, or just lower cholesterol in general?

In a recent development, to check, the team removed those cells from mice and replaced them with cells that had been treated with pantethine beforehand. The mice with pre-treated cells still got less disease.

Industry observers note that why would a vitamin relative quiet an immune cell? Zhang’s team traced it to cholesterol.

When Vanin is busy and pantethine runs low, dendritic cells make more cholesterol and pack it into their outer membranes.

Industry observers note that cholesterol-rich patches of membrane are where the cells’ alarm receptors cluster. A cell with more of those patches responds harder to the signals that switch it on.

Recent findings suggest that pantethine reversed that. Cells treated with it carried less cholesterol in their membranes and fewer clustered receptors, and they sent weaker signals through the inflammatory pathways that drive the disease.

Dendritic cells taken from psoriasis and lupus patients and treated in the dish behaved the same way.

High blood cholesterol is already known to make psoriasis worse and its treatments less effective, the authors wrote, which is what made a cholesterol-lowering supplement worth trying in people.

Sources indicate that the team enrolled 27 people with mild plaque psoriasis at the Chinese PLA General Hospital and randomly assigned them to two treatment groups. The 12-week analysis included 24 participants.

Sources indicate that everyone used a standard prescription ointment that combines a vitamin D relative with a steroid. Half also took a 300-milligram pantethine capsule twice a day, from a brand sold over the counter.

Two dermatologists scored each patient’s skin from photographs at the start, at eight weeks and at 12 weeks, using the two scales psoriasis trials usually rely on. The trial is registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry.

It has been revealed that over 12 weeks, the group taking pantethine improved more on both scales than the group using ointment alone. The dermatologists didn’t record any side effects tied to the treatment.

The difference was concentrated in people who started the trial with abnormal blood fats.

Among them, the pantethine group’s lipid profiles improved and their skin scores at 12 weeks were clearly better than those of similar patients on ointment alone.

Among patients whose blood fats were normal to begin with, the two groups ended up about the same, so the capsule didn’t add much.

The split fits the mechanism, the authors wrote, but it also narrows the finding.

“We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins,” Zhang mentioned.

Twelve people took the supplement, at one hospital, for three months, and the comparison group took no placebo capsule. Whether the gain holds up in a larger, blinded trial over a longer period is the first open question.

Sources indicate that the mechanism was worked out in mice and in cells. Other immune cells may have helped the patients improve, the authors wrote. And what switches Vanin on in the first place is still unknown.

Vanin shows up in many kinds of cells, not only dendritic cells, and the team wrote that the pathway may matter in other inflammatory diseases.

Beyond psoriasis, though, the evidence so far is a pattern in patient data, not a test in a disease model.

The next step the authors described is to test the pathway in those other diseases.

Whether people with normal blood fat levels can get anything from the supplement is a question this trial could not answer.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Experimental Medicine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The only thing worse than discovering your car has a dead battery is having it happen when it’s raining. If you live in a wet environment as I do in Oregon, you’ll be glad you own a portable jump starter like the Noco Boost Plus GB40. With its three watertight ports closed, it’s impervious to dust intrusion—but more importantly, its IP65 rating means it can withstand heavy rain and even low-pressure blasts with a hose.

In a recent development, besides its consummate performance in wet conditions, the GB40 is worth considering because it’s compact, lightweight (just over 2 pounds), and relatively easy to use. I also appreciate that it includes spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection, an output port for charging portable electronics, and a six-mode flashlight.

It has been revealed that that stated, the GB40 isn’t perfect. While I found that it punched above its weight in jump-starting power and its battery life is adequate, it isn’t the most powerful portable jump starter among those I’ve recently tested, and its 2,150 milliampere-hour (mAh) capacity is definitely on the lower side. It also doesn’t have an LED screen but rather uses lights as indicators of its status and operation. Even more crucially, it uses a manual override function to boost severely depleted batteries instead of a dedicated boost button.

I tested the Noco Boost Plus GB40 over several months in Oregon spanning the wet and dry seasons. When testing a portable jump starter, I evaluate how quickly it starts a vehicle, how many jump-starts it provides before needing to be recharged, how easy it is to use, its features, and the number and effectiveness of its auxiliary power ports to charge portable devices such as a smartphone.

The Noco GB40 easily fits in the palm of my hand, and the rubberized case and ribs built into each side make it easy to grip, which is important when working around an engine with moving parts. Its small size also means it’s easier to store in a vehicle’s glove box than a larger device like the Gooloo GT6000, which I recommend as the best portable jump starter for most people.

It has been revealed that the Noco GB40 doesn’t have an LED screen like many of the portable jump starters from Gooloo, its main competitor. But the touch-based control panel on one side makes it relatively simple to operate. This consists of a large power button with a white on/off LED next to it, a four-segment multicolor battery-level indicator that demonstrates the state of charge in 25 percent increments, an error indicator, a boost LED, a manual override button, and a button for the flashlight.

Sources indicate that with a peak output of only 1,000 amps, the Noco Boost Plus GB40 is the least powerful portable jump starter among those I’ve tested. Its 2,150 mAh rating also makes it the lowest in reserve-power capacity. That stated, it had no issues jump-starting my Honda Element when I left the lights on and drained the battery. It even cranked the 6.8-liter V10 in my RV when I came back to it after months in storage and found the battery depleted.

I also intentionally left it powered on (since it doesn’t have an automatic shutoff like the Astro AI S8, which I recommend for its value) and it lasted about 24 hours before shutting down. Via a 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-C input, it charges about as fast as other portable jump starters with the same specs, and it took just under four hours to charge from 0 to 100 percent using the supplied USB-C cable.

It has been revealed that among features, the flashlight on the GB40 is the most compelling. It has six modes, including an SOS and strobe, which puts it well ahead of the competition. It also has two lenses, one on each side of the output ports, whereas most portable jump starters use a single flashlight lens. While the flashlight isn’t as bright as some others at 100 lumens (for comparison, the $70 Gooloo GP2000, has a 400-lumen flashlight), I found the Noco GB40 more than adequate for use at night.

Industry observers note that the Noco GB40’s USB-C charging input doesn’t double as an output port to charge portable devices, which puts it at a disadvantage. It has just one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging portable electronics (the Gooloo GP2000 has two) and charged my iPhone 16 from 0 percent to 80 percent in about two hours.

Instead of a boost button that supplies a bit more amperage to jump-start a very dead battery, the GB40 has a manual override button that, when pushed and held for three seconds, detects a severely depleted battery (below three volts).

It’s a far less user-friendly feature, plus it disables the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection. As such, people need to be extra careful not to allow the cable clamps to touch, which can cause dangerous sparking. To complicate things further, the GB40 has an LED labeled “boost” that’s simply an indicator light to let you know the device is properly connected to the battery.

There are certainly much more powerful portable jump starters than the Noco Boost Plus GB40 and much of the competition offers features that are far more convenient (albeit for a higher price point), perhaps most significantly, a boost button. Above all, the GB40’s waterproof rating is the best reason to buy it, plus its compact size, six-mode flashlight, and emergency charging for small devices make it an appealing choice. It also provides ample and reliable power to give a dead battery in most vehicles a boost and start the engine.

Shop Noco Boost Plus GB40 Portable Jump Starter.

Other Portable Jump Starters We Recommend.

The Gooloo GT6000 packs 27,000 mAh of reserve power capacity and 6,000-amp peak current. This allows it to jump-start vehicles ranging from a small motorcycle to a heavy-duty truck with a 12.0-liter diesel engine. The GT6000 offers a standby time of two years, and it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after just seven minutes of recharging. It’s got a heap of charging ports, including a 100-watt USB-C in/out that can top off the internal battery from empty to full in 1.4 hours. The device’s 3.2-inch screen makes checking battery level, charging output, and more easy and foolproof.

In a recent development, with 4,000 amps of peak current and 24,000 mAh of capacity, the Wolfbox can jump-start up to 10.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines. It holds a charge for more than a year. The 1.5-cubic-foot-per-minute air pump takes one minute to inflate a 17-inch tire from 30 to 36 psi. It also has a 65-watt USB-C in/out port to quickly recharge the internal battery, two USB-A ports to charge other devices, and a 400-lumen, three-mode LED flashlight.

The Noco AX65 combines a portable jump starter and a portable air compressor into a single device. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power. The tire inflator pumps out 2.3 cubic feet per minute of airflow. The jump starter cranks gas engines up to 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. The tire inflator has a digital display, auto shutoff, and memory settings like other air compressors I’ve tested but also pauses and then resumes inflation when a set pressure is reached to ensure proper inflation.

The libido drug women want is testosterone
