  • Sources indicate that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone.
  • Industry observers note that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that these days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Industry observers note that some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

In a recent development, not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih notes. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih claims—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Sources indicate that interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen states.

Another outstanding question, Yih states, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Industry observers note that women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen presently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for latest treatments is there, Rowen states. “Women deserve better than placebo.”.

#88637. Industry News: Millions of immune cells reveal hidden links between genes and disease

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (935 w)

Industry News: Millions of immune cells reveal hidden links between genes and disease

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By measuring gene activity in 5.4 million immune cells, researchers uncovered genetic clues to disease that whole-blood studies had missed.
  • A blood sample is usually read as one mixture, and for years the studies linking genes to disease have read it that way too.
  • Yet a gene’s tie to a disease can be found in one kind of immune cell and nowhere else, so a whole-blood reading misses it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By measuring gene activity in 5.4 million immune cells, researchers uncovered genetic clues to disease that whole-blood studies had missed.

A blood sample is usually read as one mixture, and for years the studies linking genes to disease have read it that way too.

Yet a gene’s tie to a disease can be found in one kind of immune cell and nowhere else, so a whole-blood reading misses it.

Researchers sequenced each participant’s genome and measured gene activity in more than 5 million immune cells, one cell at a time.

About half of the effects linked to common genetic variants indicated up in only one or a few cell types.

That is the main result of the first phase of a project called TenK10K, which aims to build the same map for 10,000 people.

The study’s senior authors included Joseph Powell of the Garvan Institute of Medical Research and UNSW Sydney and Daniel MacArthur of the Centre for Population Genomics.

The center is a joint initiative of Garvan and the Murdoch Children’s Research Institute.

The work is a map of associations rather than a test of any treatment. Every participant was of European ancestry.

“Most of the biological mechanisms we uncovered were invisible to prior studies,” Powell said.

The team took blood from 1,925 Australian adults who had joined two earlier studies, one of eye health in Tasmania and one of heart disease in Sydney.

They sequenced each person’s whole genome. Then they measured which genes were switched on in each of 5.4 million immune cells and sorted the cells into 28 types.

Comparing people’s DNA with gene activity in each cell type showed which genetic variants turn a gene up or down, and in which cells.

They found common variants affecting 83% of the 21,404 genes they tested.

Whole-genome sequencing also let them see rare variants, which the DNA chips used in most earlier studies read poorly. Rare variants left signals on 47% of the genes, more than 30,000 effects in all.

About half of the common-variant effects appeared in only one or a few of the 28 cell types.

It has been revealed that almost none appeared in all of them. A whole-blood study averages signals across cell types, so it can miss effects that appear in only one or a few.

The team compared their map with the largest whole-blood study of this kind.

That study drew on more than 30,000 people and found roughly 17,000 genes whose activity was associated with genetic variants. The single-cell map found about the same number using data from 1,925 people.

About a quarter of the genes in the single-cell map (4,572) were absent from the whole-blood study’s list.

“This is the most detailed map to date of how genetic variation shapes the immune system,” MacArthur mentioned.

The team then matched their map against known genetic risk regions for 16 diseases, among them asthma, autoimmune conditions, cancers and infections, and for 44 blood traits from UK Biobank.

Where a risk variant and a gene-activity variant turned out to be the same one, that gene became a candidate cause.

Industry observers note that nearly 1,500 genes were tied to the diseases this way. Of all the genes tied to a disease or a blood trait, 893 had no reported genetic effect on their activity in the significant whole-blood study.

Industry observers note that A gene called OSM is the example the team keeps coming back to. It is switched on in 20 of the 28 cell types.

Its link to inflammatory bowel disease, though, appears only in natural killer cells, where the OSM gene was more active in people carrying the risk variant.

The same matching tied a gene called IGHG4 to Alzheimer’s disease in one cell type only, memory B cells.

Sources indicate that in an email interview with Earth.com, the Garvan team was asked which finding surprised them most. They pointed to “how often the link to disease sits in just one type of immune cell.”.

A gene can be active across the immune system yet connect to disease in a single cell type, they wrote. “Earlier whole-blood studies simply couldn’t see that.”.

A map like this names candidate genes and the cells they act in. It does not show that changing a gene changes the disease, and no drug was tested.

The authors also wrote that their cutoff for calling an effect cell-specific is conservative, with no second dataset of the same size to check it against.

“This first phase focused on people of European ancestry, and we want our findings to apply to everyone,” the team told Earth.com.

As the project grows, they wrote, more people will let them detect rarer genetic variants and study rarer cells.

“In the next few years, the biggest impact will be on drug discovery rather than in the clinic,” they wrote.

Drugs backed by human genetic evidence are more likely to succeed in trials, they added, and over time the map could help match patients to treatments.

Which of the nearly 1,500 candidate genes actually drive disease is the open question, and this map can’t answer it on its own.

The summary data are free for other researchers to use, and two companion papers add layers on repeated DNA and on which stretches of DNA are open in each cell.

Someone still has to run the experiments that switch a candidate gene off in the right cell type.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#88636. Latest Update: Could intermittent fasting help reverse diabetes? A new study offers a clue

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1384 w)

Latest Update: Could intermittent fasting help reverse diabetes? A new study offers a clue

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intermittent fasting helped diabetic mice restore normal blood sugar by improving insulin production without requiring extra calorie cuts.
  • In a upcoming study of mice with diet-induced diabetes, two feeding regimens produced different results even though the mice consumed about the same number of calories.
  • The difference was seen in beta cells, the pancreas cells that make insulin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intermittent fasting helped diabetic mice restore normal blood sugar by improving insulin production without requiring extra calorie cuts.

In a upcoming study of mice with diet-induced diabetes, two feeding regimens produced different results even though the mice consumed about the same number of calories.

The difference was seen in beta cells, the pancreas cells that make insulin.

One group had unlimited access to regular chow, which contained fewer calories per gram.

It has been revealed that A second group was given fatty food on alternate days. Both groups consumed about the same number of calories and ended at the same weight.

Yet blood sugar returned to normal only in the every-other-day group.

The difference emerged even though the two groups consumed about the same number of calories.

Recent findings suggest that the mice fed every other day stored more insulin in their beta cells. The researchers think fasting days gave those cells a break.

The research was conducted at Michigan Medicine, the University of Michigan’s academic medical center.

Peter Arvan, a professor of internal medicine, led the study.

Arvan is also a member of the Caswell Diabetes Institute. Research investigator Maroof Alam was the first author.

Industry observers note that all of the mice were male. Each carried a gene change that makes it prone to diabetes on a fatty diet.

Industry observers note that insulin is first made as a longer molecule that is not yet finished. It has to fold into the right shape before it can work. Biologists call it proinsulin.

Mice carry four copies of the genes that make it. In these mice, one copy had been altered. As a result, some of their proinsulin was prone to folding wrong.

Recent findings suggest that on regular food, the mice don’t need treatment. Young males that gain weight on a high-fat diet, however, develop diabetes quickly. Females are resistant, so only males were studied.

Industry observers note that from 5 to 11 weeks of age, the males were fed chow with 60% of its calories from fat. By the end, every mouse had diabetes. Their blood sugar was above 250 mg/dL at a random check.

Industry observers note that people with a change at the same spot in the insulin molecule also develop diabetes. In those patients, diet plays an important part in when it starts and how it progresses.

Sources indicate that after those six weeks, the diabetic mice were moved onto newly introduced diets for five weeks. Littermates were alternated between the two main groups.

Recent findings suggest that fifteen mice switched to regular lab chow, which gets about 14% of its calories from fat. These mice could eat as much as they liked every day.

Fifteen more stayed on the high-fat food but could eat only every other day. This pattern is a form of intermittent fasting. At noon, each mouse was moved to a fresh cage. The cage held either plenty of food or none.

It has been revealed that five more mice kept eating the high-fat diet every day. Those mice gained more weight, and their diabetes got worse.

Both diet groups ate fewer calories than before, and both stopped gaining weight. Neither group actually lost any. By the end, their body weights matched, and so did the energy they burned.

It has been revealed that insulin sensitivity also improved equally in both groups. This measure reveals how well the body’s cells respond to insulin.

Ten days in, both groups handled a dose of sugar the same way. By five weeks, however, the every-other-day mice cleared sugar from their blood better.

Industry observers note that these mice also reached normal levels on both standard blood sugar checks. One check was taken at a random time, and the other after a fast. The mice on daily chow did not reach normal levels.

“In the end, both groups of diabetic mice consumed and burned the same number of calories,” Alam said. “However, mice that were fed on alternate days had more insulin in their beta cells.”.

According to recent reports, insulin sensitivity couldn’t explain the gap, because the two groups matched on it. Insulin supply could. More insulin was found in the blood of the every-other-day mice. Their ratio of insulin to blood sugar was four times that of the chow group.

It has been revealed that beta cells sit in small clusters called islets. Islets from the every-other-day mice held more than 85% more insulin than those from the chow group. When high sugar was added, more insulin was released from these islets as well.

The islets weren’t any bigger. Under an electron microscope, though, more insulin packets were seen in beta cells from the every-other-day mice. These tiny packets are where finished insulin is stored.

The researchers also compared insulin and blood sugar at the end of a feeding day and at the end of a fasting day.

The every-other-day mice were also checked at the end of a day without food.

By then, their average blood sugar had dropped by at least 45%. Insulin in the blood fell too. This drop suggests the beta cells were sending out less insulin.

Industry observers note that yet the insulin stored in their islets was about the same after fasting and feeding days. The cells released plenty after meals without running low. So they must have been replacing what they sent out.

“We wanted to see whether rest periods between meals allow the pancreas to recover from the stress of previous meals,” Arvan mentioned.

It has been revealed that inside the cells, more proinsulin was being made in the every-other-day mice. A chemical signal known to slow proinsulin production was found at lower levels in their islets.

In a recent development, cells usually make more of a certain protein when misfolded proteins accumulate. In these mice, levels of that protein did not increase. The extra proinsulin, it seems, was produced without added stress on the cells.

In both diet groups, proinsulin was found in the same share of islet cells. The two groups probably had similar numbers of beta cells, then.

What changed with fasting, it appears, was the maturity of the existing beta cells and not their number.

Sources indicate that the two foods were not identical apart from fat. Regular chow and high-fat chow also contain different amounts of protein. They may differ in vitamins and other compounds too. The authors themselves flagged these differences in the paper.

Recent findings suggest that every animal in the study was a male mouse carrying the same insulin gene change. The results have not been tested in females or in other forms of diabetes.

In a recent development, the authors also cited earlier work in people that found related results. In one human study, insulin fell further with modified alternate-day fasting than with similar calorie cutting on no set schedule.

In a separate trial of adults with metabolic syndrome, fasting blood sugar fell more with modified alternate-day fasting than with daily calorie restriction.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases says scientists are still studying fasting in diabetes.

Its advice for doctors is that patients with type 2 diabetes who fast should have their medications watched closely.

The mice in this study started their upcoming diets after six weeks of high-fat eating. A separate set of mice stayed on the fatty diet for 11 weeks. By that point, far less insulin was left in their islets.

Animals this sick, the authors wrote, might already be beyond the point where every-other-day feeding can restore their islets.

“You need to have restoration of functional beta cells, but when diabetes is advanced, there might not be enough remaining beta cells to restore,” Arvan said.

In the paper, the authors also suggested that more than five weeks of fasting days might raise beta-cell maturity further.

“On the other hand, even though it might take longer to fix more severe stages of diabetes, we need to test if intermittent fasting can help,” he noted.

For now, the result has only been shown in young male mice whose diabetes was treated early.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Metabolism.

Scorpion fossil from an Alabama coal mine has strikingly modern features

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tiny scorpion fossil from Alabama reveals that modern scorpion features existed more than 300 million years ago.
  • It has been revealed that the world before the dinosaurs is remembered for its oversized millipedes, scorpions and dragonfly relatives.
  • The fossil appears to be the oldest known North American scorpion with breathing openings arranged like those of living scorpions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tiny scorpion fossil from Alabama reveals that modern scorpion features existed more than 300 million years ago.

It has been revealed that the world before the dinosaurs is remembered for its oversized millipedes, scorpions and dragonfly relatives. A small scorpion pulled from an old Alabama coal mine looks a lot like the ones alive today.

The fossil appears to be the oldest known North American scorpion with breathing openings arranged like those of living scorpions.

A comparably early example, complete enough to compare, had previously been reported only from the British Midlands.

The study was led by Genevieve Conway, an honours student in paleontology at Flinders University in Australia. Russell Bicknell of Flinders served as senior author.

With just one incomplete specimen to work from, the authors did not assign it to a known species.

“Well before dinosaurs roamed the planet, the scorpions, millipedes and dragonfly relatives of 315-320 million years ago were generally much larger than they are today,” Conway said.

“That is why we suspect this fossil could be a juvenile, and one of the first of its kind to be examined and connected to the evolution of modern scorpions on the North American continent.”.

Its home rock is the Pottsville Formation, laid down in humid tropics about 10 degrees south of the equator.

That places it in the Carboniferous Period, the coal-forming age. The beds at this locality are roughly 316 million to 319 million years old.

Union Chapel Mine, in Walker County, is now called the Steven C. Minkin Paleozoic Footprint Site. Scientists and volunteers helped save the old pit from being filled in after mining ended.

Recent findings suggest that two slabs were involved. One half of the split rock turned up on April 23, 2022, and the other a week later.

Recent findings suggest that both were found lying on the surface by T. Prescott Atkinson of The University of Alabama Museums, who gave them to the museum.

It has been revealed that almost everything collected at Union Chapel comes out of spoil heaps. Exactly which layer held this scorpion is unknown.

No fossil scorpion had ever been reported from the southeastern United States. The slabs were photographed at the American Museum of Natural History in Latest York.

Ordinary light came first. Then the team switched to ultraviolet, and the belly plates lit up orange while the back plates stayed dark.

Living scorpions famously glow under ultraviolet light too. Here, though, the orange comes from coal-like material that formed as the shell was altered by heat.

Three plates revealed something else under the lamp: tiny dark dots, each one rimmed in brighter orange. Conway’s team reads them as breathing holes.

In a recent development, in today’s scorpions such openings sit mid-plate on rectangular belly segments. In some ancient groups they are thought to have opened at the rear margin.

Where they fall on the Alabama fossil is what links it to the modern group.

Paired, curving lines on the same plates may be traces of book lungs. Air enters these organs through the holes.

Recent findings suggest that good evidence of book lungs is scarce, and all of it comes from older animals. Later fossils from that era have yielded none.

Preservation or simple oversight might explain the gap, according to the authors.

According to recent reports, the whole fossil is about 0.9 inch (22 millimeters) long. A quarter is a bit wider.

It has been revealed that its claws reach forward and the body bends slightly. To paleontologists those are telltale features of a molt, not a carcass.

That is the usual story; most fossil scorpions are molts.

Scorpions shed repeatedly as juveniles, which is why the team thinks this individual was young.

It has been revealed that shedding may also have destroyed the plates around the leg bases. Unfortunately, those are the plates used to sort fossils into families.

Chemically, the shell is now nearly pure carbon, the product of millions of years of heating.

According to recent reports, sulfur and calcium turned up in small amounts. Most likely they leached in from the shale around it.

The tail’s last segment, the one that connects to the stinger, is noticeably longer than those before it.

Sources indicate that most scorpions from the Silurian through the Carboniferous had tail segments of about equal length. The longer final segment shows up later and is still present today.

Industry observers note that longer segments go with longer, faster muscles, the authors wrote. That may have allowed the scorpion to sting faster.

It has been revealed that slim pincers paired with a thick tail complete the picture. In modern scorpions that build points to animals that rely on venom for hunting and defense.

They lean less on strong pincers to subdue prey.

“Remarkably, this species appears very similar to the characteristics of scorpions alive today, including those in Australia,” Conway noted.

“In fact, it probably looked really similar to Lychas, a species commonly seen by bushwalkers in Australia.”.

The team proposes that the lengthened segment evolved under pressure from predators such as early relatives of reptiles and mammals.

Those animals were diversifying at the time and were common around the site.

Before this discovery, the scorpions of Union Chapel were known only through trackways that researchers attributed to them. The body fossil lends support to that view.

“It’s the first fossil scorpion from this understudied site where lots of trackways have been found, including other fossils, by amateur fossickers and researchers,” Bicknell said.

Recent findings suggest that the fit is imperfect, though. Trackways at the site span about 0.6 to 0.9 inch (15 to 22 millimeters) in width.

The fossil’s body, by contrast, measures only about 0.16 inch (4 millimeters) across.

Leg spread could not be estimated, so the team cannot say whether an animal this size made any tracks.

Trails of varying width may have been left by scorpions of several sizes. That assumes scorpions made them at all.

It has been revealed that scorpions are the oldest arachnids in the fossil record, dating back at least 435 million years. At least one early species was a giant.

Some 170 extinct species have been described so far, against 2,918 that are living today.

Many fossil species rest on a single specimen, occasionally little more than a pincer. Others proved to be one animal described under several names.

Sources indicate that the Alabama scorpion adds a body to that record but not a name. Its side eyes and the plates beside its legs, which would indicate a family, were not preserved.

It has been revealed that it does differ from the only other scorpion known from the Pottsville rocks. That species, from Indiana, has belly plates with lobed edges.

Bicknell noted more discoveries will be made as fossils are shared with museum collections.

A second specimen with an intact underside could show which kind of scorpion lived here over 300 million years ago.

The full study was published in the journal The Science of Nature.

Breaking: Helping sick students stay home could matter for an entire campus

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Encouraging sick college students to stay home for three days may help reduce the spread of flu-like illnesses.
  • Industry observers note that staying home when sick is advice that most people have heard many times over.
  • A campus trial now suggests that a polite request to stay in may help limit the spread of illness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Encouraging sick college students to stay home for three days may help reduce the spread of flu-like illnesses.

Industry observers note that staying home when sick is advice that most people have heard many times over. College students are known to attend class while ill anyway, according to earlier research on campus health.

A campus trial now suggests that a polite request to stay in may help limit the spread of illness.

Students with flu-like symptoms in that trial were encouraged to remain in their dorm rooms for three days.

Sources indicate that nobody was forced to comply with the request. Snacks and drinks were delivered by trial staff so that staying in would be easier for sick students.

The analysis was led by Brian Richardson, a statistician at Wake Forest University.

Richardson worked with Allison Aiello of the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health. Michael Hudgens of the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health was also involved.

Recent findings suggest that the authors describe the evidence as moderate. The data also come from a single campus.

“It seems like almost every day in class, at least one person is sick,” noted Richardson.

The data were gathered in eX-FLU, a trial led by Aiello during the 2013 flu season. The trial was carried out at a large public university.

College campuses can be particularly vulnerable to outbreaks of flu-like illness. Crowded housing and large social gatherings are the main reasons given by the authors.

A total of 579 students from six residence halls were enrolled in the trial. Many of them were recruited through friends who had already joined.

Sources indicate that the six halls were split into 112 residential clusters for the purposes of the trial. Each cluster was then randomly assigned to an intervention arm or to a control arm.

Students in the intervention arm were encouraged to isolate in their rooms for 72 hours after their symptoms began.

Trial staff also helped those students notify professors and employers about any days they would miss.

No advice about isolation was given to students in the control arm at any point during the trial. Participants were asked to file weekly reports during the 10-week study.

Each report recorded whether the student had flu-like symptoms that week and which students they had met face to face. Reported cases were confirmed by trial staff.

According to recent reports, flu-like illness is defined by symptoms alone. Other respiratory infections can therefore fall under the same label as influenza.

Industry observers note that among 93 students, researchers recorded 113 cases of flu-like illness. Of these, 44 occurred in the group that received isolation advice and 69 in the control group.

However, counting cases alone could not reveal how well the advice worked. Isolation was meant to protect others rather than the sick student.

Students from both groups lived in the same residence halls and shared friends. Isolation in one group could therefore prevent infections in the other.

Instead, researchers counted every reported face-to-face meeting between sick students and other participants as a possible opportunity for infection. They could not directly track whether the illness actually spread.

Sources indicate that suppose the advice had done nothing. In that case, students in the encouraged arm should have accounted for about 48.6% of these risky meetings. Instead, they accounted for 35.9%.

Sick students who were asked to stay in were behind a smaller share of the meetings where illness could spread.

It has been revealed that A gap at least this large would still appear about 8% of the time if the advice made no difference. That figure is above the 5% cutoff that many scientists use for a firm result.

Even so, the authors concluded that encouraging sick students to stay in may have prevented flu-like illness in the trial.

In a recent development, A separate look at the students’ reported contacts pointed in the same direction. Here, sick students in the two arms were compared. Those in the encouraged arm were less likely to start or keep up face-to-face contact.

“Even though students were simply encouraged – not required – to stay home when sick, and not everyone followed the recommendation perfectly, the intervention still appears to have reduced disease transmission,” Richardson said.

Students in eX-FLU were linked to one another through their dorms, their friendships and the way they were recruited.

Most standard statistical methods are designed for people who have no such links to each other. A fresh testing procedure was therefore developed by Richardson and Hudgens for the eX-FLU data.

Recent findings suggest that the procedure was built to check for an effect on infections, not just on social contacts. Fewer contacts would offer little public health benefit if the number of infections stayed the same.

Its performance was tested first on 10,000 simulated trials in each of three scenarios.

Physical distancing has well-documented downsides, according to the paper.

Mental health problems, economic hardship, disrupted schooling and poorer access to health care are all listed. Vulnerable populations are described as especially exposed to those harms.

Recent findings suggest that mandatory isolation is described in the paper as more invasive and more difficult to carry out. Newly introduced vaccines can take months or years to develop, the researchers remarked.

Encouragement to isolate was described as something that could be introduced rapidly in response to new outbreaks.

“People are much more likely to stay home when they’re sick if we make it possible for them to do so,” remarked Aiello.

“Our findings suggest that encouraging voluntary isolation – and supporting it with simple resources like meal delivery and basic supplies – can help reduce disease transmission without requiring more restrictive public health measures.”.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention already tells people with respiratory viruses to stay home while sick.

Sources indicate that staying in after symptoms start leaves a gap, since flu can spread for a day or two before symptoms show. With COVID-19, spread before or without symptoms is even more common.

In a recent development, all of the contact data in eX-FLU came from weekly surveys filled out by the students themselves. Infected students listed more contacts than healthy ones, and the authors raised recall bias as one possible explanation.

Recent findings suggest that transmission itself was never observed in the trial. Only meetings between a sick student and another student could be counted.

Recent findings suggest that the test can show whether the three-day request had an effect. It was not designed to measure how large that effect was.

All 579 students were part of one connected network on a single campus. Comparisons with other strategies could not readily be made with the eX-FLU data.

A larger sample or a different test statistic might have yielded stronger evidence, according to the authors.

A subset of students in the trial were given smartphones through a side project called iEpi. Those phones recorded when two students were near each other.

Bluetooth data of this kind could be used to correct the self-reported contacts.

Sources indicate that the length of the request is another open question. A six-day version was considered in a pilot of eX-FLU. Pilot participants said they would be less likely to follow the longer request.

Future studies could compare several isolation periods and record both adherence and infections for each.

Trials on separate campuses could also test whether encouraging every student beats targeting only high-risk individuals.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for latest member orientation on Monday.
  • What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?
  • As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for latest member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

In a recent development, trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s upcoming member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

Sources indicate that “I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” noted Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Industry observers note that forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

“I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he said of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”.

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

“It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” remarked Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

It has been revealed that “The congressman stated that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s key that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke noted. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

“I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” stated Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

But just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” mentioned Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

It has been revealed that “I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he noted.

After arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander said he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he said.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their upcoming workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” said Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

Sources indicate that “They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the Fresh Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

#88628. Tech Report: Why do some images stick in your memory while others fade?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1329 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why do some images stick in your memory while others fade?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recordings inside the amygdala show which pictures a person will remember, flagged within a third of a second of first seeing them.
  • You can look at two pictures for the same length of time and, minutes later, recognize only one.
  • Some cells deep in the brain fired more strongly for pictures people later recognized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recordings inside the amygdala show which pictures a person will remember, flagged within a third of a second of first seeing them.

You can look at two pictures for the same length of time and, minutes later, recognize only one. In a upcoming experiment, that difference highlighted up in the brain about a third of a second after each picture appeared.

Some cells deep in the brain fired more strongly for pictures people later recognized. Those cells sit in the amygdala, a structure better known for fear.

Jiayang Xiao and Ueli Rutishauser of Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles led the work.

They collaborated with colleagues at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, Toronto Western Hospital, and the University of Toronto.

Everyone in the study had drug-resistant epilepsy and was already wired with electrodes, so surgeons could find where the seizures start. The memory test was a run of photographs on a screen, not anything from daily life.

“Our results demonstrate that the activity of specific kinds of neurons in the amygdala predicts, while the person sees an image for the first time, whether that image will later be remembered,” said Rutishauser, who directs the Center for Neural Science and Medicine at Cedars-Sinai.

“Such episodic autobiographical memories, such as where we parked our car or how we spent a recent family vacation, are critical to navigating everyday life and a sense of who we are.”.

It has been revealed that the amygdala’s reputation comes from fear and feeling. People with damage on both sides of it remember emotional material poorly.

Brain scans going back to the 1990s found that the harder the amygdala worked while someone studied an emotional picture, the better that person held onto it.

So the working explanation was feeling. A strong reaction marks a moment as worth keeping, and the amygdala supplies the reaction.

Recent findings suggest that xiao’s team asked something narrower. Instead of the amygdala’s overall activity, they tracked single neurons that each answer to one kind of thing.

One cell fires for faces and ignores cars. Another fires for landscapes and ignores food. These are called category cells, and 40% of the amygdala neurons here were one.

It has been revealed that the two explanations predict different things. If feeling is the mark, a jolt should lift every cell at once. If the content of the moment is the mark, only the cells tuned to that content should move.

The electrodes used for seizure monitoring carry eight hair-thin wires at the tip. That is fine enough to hear one neuron at a time.

Sources indicate that across 49 sessions with 42 patients, the team logged 1,871 well-isolated neurons. Of those, 575 were in the amygdala and 405 in the hippocampus, the region usually given credit for building memories.

In a recent development, the task was plain. Photographs from five categories – people, food, animals, cars and landscapes – came up for two seconds each, and all of them were latest to the patient.

Ten to 30 minutes later came a test of 400 images. Half had been in the earlier run and half had never been seen.

Six buttons were available for each one. Three remarked newly introduced and three said old, and the button within each set said how sure the patient was. Patients got 70.3% right, against 50% for guessing.

When patients first saw the pictures, category cells in the amygdala fired more strongly for images the patients later recognized than for those they didn’t.

The effect held only when the picture belonged to the cell’s own category.

Recent findings suggest that A cell tuned to faces fired more strongly for faces the patient later recognized. When the patient saw a car, that same cell’s activity gave no clue about whether the patient would recognize it later.

The difference in firing appeared about 350 milliseconds after the picture came into view and lasted until about 1,850 milliseconds.

The cells started responding to their preferred category at around 300 milliseconds, just before the first signs of which pictures patients would remember.

The effect held after researchers accounted for an online panel’s ratings of how pleasant and exciting the images were.

The ratings alone did not predict which pictures patients later recognized.

According to recent reports, the first dataset also demonstrated a weaker hippocampal signal that emerged around 1,300 milliseconds. In sessions that recorded both regions, the amygdala’s signal was stronger.

Rutishauser told Earth.com that the amygdala finding surprised him because the region is best known for responding to emotionally charged experiences. Here, its activity predicted which neutral images patients would later recognize.

The fusiform gyrus is a patch of visual cortex where two-thirds of the neurons were category cells, the highest share anywhere in the study.

It demonstrated no such split between the pictures that were remembered and the ones that were not. Strong tuning by itself does not do this.

For the kind of memory tested here, Rutishauser remarked, the memory itself is stored in the hippocampus, and the amygdala works more like a controller.

“The system that produces the hot air (the heater) is separate and distinct from the controller (the thermostat),” he noted to Earth.com. “In analogy, here the amygdala would be the thermostat that controls the memory system.”.

In a recent development, the two regions were also in step. Slow electrical waves run through the hippocampus at around 10 cycles a second.

Amygdala cells fired more tightly in time with those waves when a picture was going to be remembered than when it was going to be forgotten.

According to recent reports, A second set of recordings, from 95 other patients and 5,744 neurons, carried the amygdala result again. The hippocampal effect did not come back in that one.

Among the pictures patients did recognize, the ones they felt sure about had drawn more firing at first sight than the ones they guessed at.

Sources indicate that the team then split each patient’s hits into two kinds of remembering. There is the vivid sort, where a person gets the moment itself back, and the vague sort, where a picture only feels familiar.

The amygdala signal tracked the vivid kind, with a session-by-session correlation of 0.50. It showed no reliable link to familiarity.

According to recent reports, the effect was also stronger in the right amygdala than in the left. The authors call that part provisional and say it needs replication.

It may follow from their choice of material, since the right side of the brain is tied to remembering pictures and the left to remembering words.

In a recent development, nothing here was switched on or off. Every number is a prediction read off a recording, so what the amygdala does for a memory, as opposed to what it states about one, is still open.

The hippocampal effect that showed up in one dataset and not the other is unsettled too.

The patients were also people with epilepsy severe enough to need brain surgery, and the electrodes went where their care required.

Amygdala tissue shrinks early in Alzheimer’s disease, and memory trouble is common in temporal lobe epilepsy.

Rutishauser stated the findings are still too preliminary to guide treatment for people with memory problems.

However, he also noted that the research raises the possibility that a device designed to aid memory could target the amygdala, particularly on the right side of the brain.

One possibility is that deep brain stimulation could boost the activity of cells already responding to what a person sees.

Industry observers note that the idea is untested. Earlier teams that stimulated the whole amygdala electrically improved recognition of neutral pictures, but none aimed at the category cells.

Rutishauser’s team is now studying how the amygdala coordinates with other brain regions and whether stimulating it can improve memory.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Neuroscience.

The 6 Best Mini-LED TVs Deliver a Bright Screen and Great Value

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created.
  • The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot upcoming multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Mini-LED is among the most versatile display technologies ever created. By shrinking down the LED backlighting that powered older TVs since flat screens first gained traction in the late 2000s, TV makers have found a way to deliver brighter TVs with richer, more accurate colors without relying on expensive latest display technologies.

The best mini-LED TVs right now provide a brighter and more impactful picture than ever, especially since many of them get a performance boost from other display tech like quantum dots and the hot upcoming multicolored backlight configuration, RGB LED.

Recent findings suggest that just as importantly, they often offer great bang for the buck, especially when you're looking for a larger screen size—let’s say 75 inches or higher. As malleable as they are cost-effective, mini-LED is the secret sauce behind some of the best TVs on the market, even outdoing premium OLED screens in metrics like brightness and color expansion.

We’ve tested the top mini-LED TVs around, from entry-level options to groundbreaking flagships, to help you find the best options for your money.

In a recent development, I picked the top mini-LED TVs after sampling the best the market has to offer from brands like LG, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Hisense. I tested four of the TVs directly, while two of them were tested by Popular Mechanics staff and recommended based on that testing.

It has been revealed that my evaluation was based on performance traits like brightness, color vibrancy and accuracy, image processing and upscaling, black levels, and overall contrast. For my testing process, I used objective measurements like brightness and color accuracy with a Portrait Displays C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a G1 pattern generator, and Calman software, as well as subjective testing using a wide library of familiar content, from test demos to films and TV highlights via 4K HDR Blu-rays and streaming. I also weighed usability features like smarts and gaming options, overall design, and size options for those interested in the ever-expanding big-screen TV market.

I’ve been reviewing TVs and audio technology for well over a decade at publications like Wired, Business Insider, Digital Trends, and others. I’ve reviewed virtually every kind of TV and display technology available, from budget screens to premium RGB LEDs. I’ve gone hands-on with the best new mini-LED TVs from brands like Samsung, LG, Sony, TCL, Hisense, Roku, and others, along with competing tech like OLED and QD-OLED, each of which has its advantages. Few things give me more pleasure than finding people the best tech for their money at every performance level and budget.

RGB LED, which uses tri-colored red, green, and blue light clusters for enhanced color expression, was the hot new display tech at the start of 2026. Virtually every major brand debuted some form of RGB Mini-LED, kick-starting a premium Mini-LED alternative to OLED.

In a recent development, when TCL introduced its own RGB TV for 2026, the RM9L, it seemed less excited about the RGB factor, and more interested in hyping up its exclusive latest mini-LED tech, Super Quantum Dots (SQD). The QM8L makes it easy to see why.

Recent findings suggest that SQD is an advanced version of regular quantum dots: tiny nanocrystals that emit pure, bright colors when exposed to light to enhance colors and brightness. Fancy tech aside, the results speak for themselves. The QM8L offers incredible brightness, far outshining its predecessor, the QM8K, alongside expansive colors that are as accurate as they are vibrant.

In a recent development, the new display offers other benefits, including fantastic black levels with very little light bleed, and reduced off-angle performance loss for most settings. Image processing has also improved, getting closer to the clarity and upscaling in top flagships from brands like LG and Samsung. The result is a premium picture that comes tantalizingly close to OLED displays in terms of contrast between the lightest and darkest images, and details that seem to pull you into the screen.

The TV’s Google TV interface is another plus, offering easy setup and extras like the ability to add albums from your Google Photos library as screen savers. Modern connectivity provides top-tier gaming features across inputs, and the sound isn’t bad either, thanks to built-in Bang & Olufsen speakers. Given that you can grab a 65-inch QM8L for as low as $1,000 or less on sale, it’s an easy pick for the best mini-LED TV available.

In a recent development, in many ways, entry-level TVs like the Hisense U6SF Pro are the best way to gauge how far TV tech has come in recent years. You just don’t expect a TV this cheap to look this good, from punchy brightness and naturalistic colors to minimal light bleed that lets you watch even challenging scenes in a dark room without being pulled out of the moment.

Industry observers note that one sacrifice at this price is the TV’s black levels, which don’t look as rich as pricier mini-LED TVs, let alone self-lit OLED displays. Because of that, even though the TV’s brightness rises above anything you can stream, it can look less striking than step-up models. On the other hand, its matte-like screen does a great job of diminishing ambient light and even direct light reflections for a good picture day or night. That’s something I didn’t expect to see at this level.

You’ll get some handy features, including support for all major HDR formats and dual HDMI 2.1 ports with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) up to 144 Hz for PC gaming, another impressive get at this price. I find the TV’s Fire TV smart system a little clunky, but it includes some cool extras, like Ambient Mode that displays free artwork. TCL’s QM6K is a good alternative thanks to its friendlier Google TV smart system, but it can’t match the U6SF Pro’s performance, which is the best I’ve tested at its price point.

According to recent reports, the step-down model of our top-rated QM8L, TCL’s QM7L offers many of the same goodies that make its pricier sibling such a rock star, but at a much lower list price. It all starts with the same SQD display tech, for excellent brightness and color vibrancy, and the kind of dimensional contrast that pushes mini-LED closer to OLED.

Sources indicate that the QM7L isn’t quite as much of a powerhouse as the QM8L, but it’s still put-on-your-sunglasses bright, blasting well past anything you can stream, and properly lighting high-quality 4K HDR Blu-rays. Its potency aids in remarkable color expansion for a deep dive into advanced films like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. Importantly, the TV also provides good color accuracy, along with deep black levels for excellent contrast. You’ll still see some minor light bleed if you look for it, and picture quality is reduced off-axis, but both are relatively minor concessions, especially for the price.

The TV offers a similarly loaded set of gaming features to last year’s QM7K, including options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode) across two of its four HDMI inputs. Like the QM8L, its Google TV smart system is intuitive to set up and use. That’s all icing on a TV that comes about as close as I’ve seen to a premium display for the money.

Recent findings suggest that hisense’s mid-tier mini-LED TV doesn’t offer the latest display technologies like RGB LED or Super Quantum Dots, but it does offer seriously punchy performance, along with a design that feels much more premium than its price class suggests. That starts with Hisense’s latest anti-reflective matte screen that eliminates most ambient reflections, matched by slim bezels and a stylish pedestal stand with the kind of build quality usually reserved for flagship TVs.

Sources indicate that under the hood is a potent mini-LED display that employs regular quantum dots for rich colors and brightness that meets or beats anything in its class, including TCL’s QM7L. When paired with its rich black levels and reflection-repelling screen, you’ll have no trouble watching even darker shows in a bright room. Hisense’s image processing has also improved for enhanced detail and upscaling with low-quality content. I did notice that the TV’s local dimming may create some artifacts at its highest setting, but it’s a very minor glitch. Like most backlit TVs, it also loses some picture quality when viewed from an angle.

Feature-wise, the U7SG is a gaming master, including VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 165 Hz across all four HDMI inputs, and handy extras like an intuitive game bar for adjusting settings on the fly. Add in its snappy Google TV interface, and you’re getting a whole lot of good stuff at a price that often falls well below $1,000 for a 65-inch model, and stays competitive up to a whopping 116 inches.

It has been revealed that after skipping a year, Hisense’s flagship U9 series is back, now loaded with the latest RGB LED display tech for a striking makeover. The TV uses its tri-colored red, green, and blue mini-LED backlighting to great effect, providing rich black levels and sparkling colors that increasingly close the gap with OLED, alongside the kind of dazzling brightness that OLED can’t yet match.

The UR9’s screen gets an advanced version of Hisense’s matte-like anti-glare coating called “Obsidian,” which impressively repels ambient and even most direct light sources, making it a great option in sunlit rooms. Turn the lights off, and you’ll find great shadow detail and very little light bleed from bright objects on dark backgrounds.

Hisense outfits the TV with some premium extras, from a capable 4.1.2-channel speaker system to HDMI 2.1 support at up to 165 Hz across all three HDMI inputs. There’s also a DisplayPort for connecting a PC, though I would have liked to see a fourth HDMI 2.1 port as well. The TV has also gotten an revision for the latest advanced HDR format, Dolby Vision 2, making it well-primed for the future. It’s all wrapped in a stylish design, for a posh taste of next-gen luxury at an accessible price point.

Sources indicate that TCL was so confident in its entry-level QM6K that it was the first TV the brand released with its new mini-LED display tech in 2025, and the only major model that wasn’t replaced for 2026. That badge of honor is well earned, as the QM6K is one of the best-performing TVs I’ve tested in its price class, with naturalistic colors, rich black levels and contrast, and enough brightness to properly light up HDR scenes like a blazing sunset or a jet’s afterburners.

It has been revealed that maybe just as impressive are the complications the QM6K avoids. While most TVs in its class readily reveal issues like screen aberrations on solid backgrounds, light bleed from bright images, and awful off-angle performance, the QM6K mostly stays clear of those pitfalls so you can simply enjoy the picture without distraction. My only real performance complaint is the TV’s particularly bad sound, but given that nearly all TVs I test are much better off with a soundbar or speaker system, that’s not a major surprise.

When it comes to extras, the QM6K is well stocked with options like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) at up to 144 Hz for blur-free action and a gaming bar to adjust features on the fly. And while the TV isn’t nearly as bright as my top budget pick, the U6SF Pro, its Google TV smart system is more intuitive and responsive for a better overall user experience. With a 55-inch model now available for under $500, the QM6K is tough to pass up.

Most TVs on this list are available from 55 inches to large-scale models at 98 inches or larger, and at increasingly reasonable price points. A big reason for that is, unlike OLED, mini-LED TVs are scalable at a relatively low cost, so screens fit for large home theaters are much more attainable. That’s one of mini-LED’s biggest advantages over other display tech, not to mention the potential for next-gen brightness and color coverage at lower pricing. That noted, ultra-large screens more readily expose performance issues, so it’s key to balance screen size with quality so you don’t regret your purchase later.

All of the TVs on this list offer 4K resolution with HDR (High Dynamic Range), and you wouldn’t want to buy a TV with lower resolution these days unless you’re looking for a very small screen (around 48 inches or lower) for a bedroom or office. The majority of newly introduced content is shot in 4K with HDR, the latter of which provides higher brightness and better contrast between the lightest and darkest images, along with the potential for more vibrant colors. Some TVs still offer 8K resolution, but because 8K content is scarce and difficult to recognize with the naked eye, it’s essentially dead (or at least dormant) in the current TV landscape.

According to recent reports, as for refresh rates, any TV with 120-Hz or higher is preferred for fast-moving content like sports and, especially, gaming. All of the TVs on this list offer 120 Hz refresh rates or higher with VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), designed to adjust to games dynamically to reduce lag and screen tearing/blur. Many TVs push to 144 Hz or better, but those refresh rates are only accessible with select gaming PCs. For consoles—PS5, Xbox Series S/X, and the Nintendo Switch 2—120 Hz is sufficient.

All of the displays on this list use mini-LED-backlighting, a smaller and more accurate version of traditional LED backlighting, paired with a liquid-crystal display (LCD). Because mini-LEDs are smaller, they can be used more prevalently to create better brightness and more dimming zones, which can enhance black levels for better contrast between the brightest and darkest images. Mini-LEDs can also be enhanced by features like quantum dots, nanoparticles that produce pure bright colors when exposed to light. Some advanced Mini-LED TVs also use RGB LED technology, which trades uniform blue or white mini-LEDs for multicolor red, green, and blue light clusters designed to produce purer, more expansive colors at the light source.

According to recent reports, in contrast (no pun intended), OLED displays use organic material excited by electricity to light each of a TV’s millions of pixels independently. These self-lit (a.k.a. self-emissive) displays have distinct advantages, including the ability to create perfect black levels for enhanced contrast over backlit displays, along with much wider viewing angles. Like mini-LEDs, some OLED displays also use quantum dots: So-called “QD-OLED” TVs offer enhanced brightness and colors, among other upcoming technologies to compete with ever-brighter and more advanced mini-LED TVs.

It has been revealed that both display types have their advantages. OLED is the best choice for those after a more balanced, nuanced, and uniform picture, especially if money isn’t a concern. However, because mini-LED is generally cheaper to produce, it may be a better choice for those on a budget who want the largest and brightest screen for their money. And in recent years, the best mini-LED TVs have increasingly advanced to better compete against OLED.

The most important connectivity option for gamers is HDMI 2.1, which offers higher bandwidth to get the most out of gaming devices. HDMI 2.1 allows for high refresh rates and features like VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) from devices like the PS5, Xbox Series X, and gaming PCs. If you’re only connecting a Blu-ray player or streaming device, HDMI 2.0 will suffice. All of the TVs on this list also support HDMI eARC/ARC, which allows you to easily connect newer soundbars and other audio devices at high resolution for enhanced audio performance.

WiFi 6 or 7 may also be helpful for wireless streaming, especially if you’re watching a lot of high-resolution content, though you’ll need a router that supports those formats. Most TVs also include an Ethernet connection for a mainline connection to your modem. Other connection options to consider include Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, ATSC 3.0 for features like over-the-air HDR from an HD antenna, and an optical connection for older audio devices like a legacy amplifier or soundbar.

All the TVs on this list come with a smart TV platform for streaming from popular apps, and many include options that let you stream content directly from a smartphone like Apple AirPlay or Google Cast. My favorite platforms are Roku and Google TV, which I find the easiest to navigate and use on a daily basis. All smart platforms collect some form of personal information, so it’s key to be careful when agreeing to terms and licensing to protect your privacy.

Sources indicate that each TV also supports multiple HDR formats, which is vital for getting the best performance. HDR10 is the baseline format, which all modern TVs support. Most TVs also support dynamic HDR formats like Dolby Vision and HDR10+ (many support both). These advanced formats can provide a more precise vision of a director’s intent by adjusting the brightest and darkest images scene by scene, and even frame by frame. Dolby Vision is the most common dynamic HDR format for streaming.

Industry observers note that if you’re interested in voice control, you’ll want to look for voice assistants like Roku Voice, Amazon Alexa or Alexa+, and Google Assistant or Gemini. If you’re connecting an audio device that supports spatial audio, like a Dolby Atmos soundbar or A/V receiver, you may also want to ensure your TV supports 3D audio formats like Dolby Atmos and, for 4K Blu-rays, DTS:X.

#88626. Southern right whales are raising calves in places scientists didn’t expect

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1073 w)

Southern right whales are raising calves in places scientists didn’t expect

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Southern right whale mothers off Australia moved to a different nursing bay 54% of the time, crowding into sites where other whales were.
  • Researchers long thought southern right whales returned to the same bay where they were nursed to raise their own calves.
  • But off southern Australia, when researchers spotted the same mother with different calves in successive sightings, she was in a different nursing area 54% of the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southern right whale mothers off Australia moved to a different nursing bay 54% of the time, crowding into sites where other whales were.

Researchers long thought southern right whales returned to the same bay where they were nursed to raise their own calves.

But off southern Australia, when researchers spotted the same mother with different calves in successive sightings, she was in a different nursing area 54% of the time.

As southern right whales recovered from whaling, mothers and calves gathered in three stretches of coast, while other apparently suitable areas drew few whales.

Researchers think the presence of other whales may help explain why those three areas grew so rapidly.

Anne Grundlehner of the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania led the work with colleagues from the Australian Antarctic Division.

Her team used nearly five decades of aerial surveys and a photo catalog that tells individual right whales apart by the rough patches of skin on their heads.

The catalog held 501 females seen with a calf in at least two different years between 1978 and 2012. Nearly two thirds, 63.5%, had nursed in more than one of the ten areas where the whales gather.

Among all 767 whales photographed in more than one year, 82.4% were seen in more than one area.

Mothers did come back to the three busiest areas more often. A mother seen in one of those three with a calf was back with her next calf 48% of the time. In the seven smaller areas, the figure was 15%.

“The results surprised us very much,” Grundlehner remarked in an interview with Earth.com.

Right whales were long believed to memorize the bay or beach where they were nursed as newborns and to return to it again and again, she remarked.

A single-engine plane has flown the coast of Western Australia each winter since 1976. The route now runs about 1,550 miles (2,500 kilometers), from Perth to Ceduna in South Australia.

Southern right whales spend summer feeding far to the south and migrate to the coast in winter.

Mothers and calves stay in water 16 to 33 feet (5 to 10 meters) deep, close to the beach.

From 1,500 feet (450 to 500 meters) up, the crew spots almost every dark whale over the pale sand, then drops lower for a photograph.

Flights run from mid-August to mid-September, when calf numbers peak, and the annual count climbed from a handful to several hundred.

In a recent development, “When the whales were still a rarity along the coastline, the few whales visiting our coast seemed randomly distributed across suitable habitat. There weren’t any sites that stood out as hotspots,” Grundlehner mentioned.

By the mid-1980s, southern right whales were gathering in three areas that filled up much faster than the rest of the coast.

The hotspots were Bremer and Doubtful Islands Bays, the stretch from Israelite Bay to Point Culver, and the Bunda Cliffs and Head of Bight.

In one of those areas, the number of mothers with calves rose by about 30% a year during the first decade.

Daughters returning to their birth bays can’t account for growth that fast. The team did the arithmetic.

With every female returning to her birth area, a calf every three years and no deaths, an area’s mothers could grow by at most 9.7% a year.

Sources indicate that which areas were busy at the start didn’t predict which became busy later, either. By a statistical measure of clumping, the whales bunched up more each year until about 2000, and the pattern has held since.

“Instead, as the population grew in numbers, the female whales were more likely to select nursing grounds where there were other whales,” mentioned co-author Stuart Corney, an associate professor at the same institute.

The team’s reading is that mothers rely on a memory of past nursing sites plus the sight or sound of other whales, a pattern also proposed for humpback whales.

The three busy areas are more open and exposed than the other bays, which the authors suggest could make other whales easier to see or hear.

When only a few dozen whales reached the coast each year, there may have been no one to follow.

It has been revealed that the whales do seem loyal to something, at a larger scale. Most repeat sightings of the same whale fell within about 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) of each other.

Grundlehner told Earth.com the findings imply more flexibility than researchers had assumed.

Grundlehner was asked what the findings mean for protecting nursing areas.

“This is extremely vital for effective conservation management: it means that you should not just protect the places with the highest numbers of an animal species you are trying to protect, but all suitable habitat that is available and accessible to them,” she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that areas used by few whales today could matter more if the population grows or if climate change alters the coast, she said. The range also needs to stay connected, with nothing blocking movement between nursing sites.

Sources indicate that growth is not guaranteed. Since about 2015, annual numbers in every area have flattened or dipped, and the population is estimated at a tenth of its pre-whaling size.

Grundlehner’s team reported in a 2025 study that recovery had stalled. She told Earth.com that calf numbers from 2023 to 2026 have stayed relatively stable, about 8% below their peak around 2016 and 2017.

The team can’t rule out other explanations for why some bays filled and others didn’t.

Records from before whaling are patchy, so it’s uncertain whether the three busy areas were busy two centuries ago.

The photo catalog also stops in 2012, so the latest decade of movements hasn’t been checked whale by whale.

And a more flexible whale isn’t necessarily a safer one. A population that follows other whales, or returns to a remembered bay, may keep using a place even after conditions there change, the authors wrote.

What draws whales to a particular bay, including local conditions and human disturbance, has to be worked out.

After that, someone has to watch whether the three crowded areas hold if the population starts growing again or shrinks further.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
