#88624. Honey bee hives can lose their most destructive pest at high altitudes

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1589 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Honey bee hives can lose their most destructive pest at high altitudes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Low oxygen levels at high altitudes prevent varroa mites from reproducing, offering a potential way to protect honeybees.
  • Sources indicate that varroa mites kill honey bee colonies around the world.
  • Sources indicate that on the Tibetan Plateau, however, hives have gone untreated since 2006.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Low oxygen levels at high altitudes prevent varroa mites from reproducing, offering a potential way to protect honeybees.

Sources indicate that varroa mites kill honey bee colonies around the world. Beekeepers fight them with chemical treatments year after year.

Sources indicate that on the Tibetan Plateau, however, hives have gone untreated since 2006. Beekeepers there report that the mites simply disappear.

At two sites above about 11,500 feet (3,500 meters), low oxygen pressure kept the mites’ young from maturing.

A lack of oxygen had never before been shown to stop the mite from breeding. The finding could lead to newly introduced ways of controlling the pest without chemicals.

The work was led by Huoqing Zheng of Zhejiang University. Researchers at the Xizang Academy of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry Sciences in Lhasa took part. So did scientists at the University of Salford in England.

Infested hives were trucked to different heights in China. The high-altitude effect was then copied in hives close to sea level.

That second test was small, with five hives over 11 days. The team also hasn’t yet worked out how low oxygen stops the mites.

“For the first time, beekeepers in Tibet noticed the parasitic varroa mite mysteriously disappear from their colonies,” the authors wrote in a statement.

“We found that the low oxygen pressure on the Tibetan Plateau prevents the mites from reproducing.”.

Sources indicate that honey bees are the most important managed pollinator of farm crops. For 60 years, Varroa destructor has been a leading cause of their deaths.

Recent findings suggest that A female mite enters a cell holding a bee larva about a day before the cell is sealed. Worker bees close it with a wax cap. Shut inside, the mite feeds on the larva. Her first egg is laid about 60 hours later.

It has been revealed that the first egg always becomes a male. The next three or four become females. They mate with their brother inside the cell.

Recent findings suggest that time in a worker bee’s cell is limited. Only the male and up to three daughters grow up before the bee emerges. Only the adult daughters can survive outside, where they live and feed on adult bees.

It has been revealed that mite populations can grow rapidly once a colony becomes infested. Viruses are also transmitted by the mites as they feed. In cooler regions this combination can kill a colony within three years.

In China, hives are treated with chemicals up to five times a year. Despite these treatments, high colony losses continue to be reported. The mite has been identified as the main cause of these losses.

Sources indicate that beekeeping on the plateau began only recently. In 2004 a total of 30 colonies were brought up to the region. Twenty years later the number of colonies had grown to more than 12,000.

In May 2024 a total of 60 colonies were taken from a single apiary in southern China. The colonies were divided into four groups of 15 for the experiment.

Sources indicate that one group was moved to another site in Xishuangbanna at roughly 1,800 feet (554 meters). The remaining three groups were transported by truck to sites located at higher elevations.

Kunming lies at roughly 6,450 feet (1,966 meters) and Nyingchi lies at roughly 9,600 feet (2,928 meters).

The highest site was Lhasa at roughly 11,900 feet (3,637 meters), more than twice the elevation of Denver.

According to recent reports, A decline in mite infestation was observed only in the Lhasa group. Before the move, mites were present in 9.3% of developing bees in the colonies headed for Lhasa.

It has been revealed that this proportion had decreased to 1.6% after four months and no mites were detected after one year. No treatment had been applied to these hives. Instead the offspring of the mites failed to reach adulthood.

An increase in infestation was recorded at the lower sites over the same period.

In Kunming, the proportion of infested bees increased from 2.8% to 21.8% within two months. Those colonies were also attacked by hornets.

The elevation of Nyingchi proved insufficient to provide protection. Infestation there increased from 3.4% to 10.6% over four months and all colonies had died within a year.

According to recent reports, by the four-month mark, 25 of the 30 colonies at the two lowest sites had died. Mites were considered the most likely cause of these losses.

In contrast, 14 of the 15 Lhasa colonies remained alive and free of mites after one year. Thirteen of these colonies survived for two years without any treatment.

To see what was going wrong, the team opened sealed cells with forceps. Each cell was checked under a flashlight, and young mites were counted in at least 218 infested cells per group.

Mother mites in Lhasa never laid more than two eggs. A second high site, tested in 2023, highlighted the same thing. Those eggs seldom developed into the next stage.

Across 178 cells with older pupae at both sites, no daughter mite was on track to become a mated adult.

It all happened fast. Just three days after the trucks arrived in Lhasa, mothers were laying far fewer eggs. By day six, each was laying one or two eggs that never developed.

The team also looked for other explanations. Bees keep the brood nest at a steady warmth whatever the weather.

Nests in both Lhasa and Xishuangbanna stayed at about 93°F to 94°F (34°C), and humidity was similar too.

Worker bees took about 21 days from egg to adult in both places, so altitude had not slowed them. The lowland colonies had been trucked as well.

Yet in Lhasa, mite breeding stayed low for months after the hives stopped moving.

It has been revealed that that left oxygen as a possible explanation. At Lhasa’s high altitude, oxygen pressure is only about two-thirds of that at sea level.

Industry observers note that A second experiment was designed to test the role of oxygen directly. Low-oxygen hives were set up in Shaoxing in eastern China at about 290 feet (88 meters) above sea level.

Sources indicate that A nitrogen-rich gas mixture was supplied from a cylinder to each of five small hives. The hives were wrapped in cling film to reduce leakage of the gas.

The flow was adjusted by hand whenever the oxygen readings moved outside the target range. The entrances were left open so that the bees could continue to forage.

In a recent development, each hive was first kept on ordinary air and then switched to air with roughly Lhasa’s oxygen level. Under ordinary air the mother mites produced an average of 3.9 offspring.

After 11 days under low oxygen this figure fell to 1.7. Almost none of these offspring developed beyond the egg stage.

Eleven days after their cells were sealed, the worker bees examined in both conditions had reached the newly emerged adult stage.

This fits with honey bees being known to forage as high as about 13,450 feet (4,100 meters). A similar decline in mite reproduction had been seen after six days in a 2023 trial with six hives.

Recent findings suggest that adult mites appear to tolerate low oxygen better than their offspring. In Lhasa the mother mites remained in the hives for several months although they could not reproduce.

It has been revealed that an adult mite breathes through two networks of air tubes. Each network opens to the outside through a single pore. Adult females have also been reported to move air through these tubes by changing their body volume.

Recent findings suggest that newly hatched mites have no air tubes at all. Instead they absorb oxygen through the skin until the first molt, when the tubes are formed.

Sources indicate that most young mites in Lhasa failed to develop beyond this first stage. The authors suggest that this feature may contribute to the vulnerability of the young. This explanation has not yet been tested.

A similar pattern has been reported in fruit flies and in a common spider mite. In both species egg production is more sensitive to low oxygen than adult survival.

In a recent development, other mechanisms may also be involved, such as the mother’s energy reserves or how cells use and sense oxygen. These possibilities are listed by the authors as questions for future work.

In a recent development, moving hives to such high elevations is not practical for most beekeepers. The team therefore tested a simple and low-cost alternative.

Recent findings suggest that hive entrances were narrowed at night so that the breathing of the bees lowered the oxygen inside. In a pilot test this method partly reduced mite reproduction. “This physiological limit of varroa mites opens upcoming avenues of controlling this globally destructive pest,” the authors wrote.

All of the results so far come from hives in China. Only one kind of bee was studied, the Italian honey bee, the type most commonly kept there.

The effect has not yet been tested in other regions or with other kinds of bees.

According to recent reports, it is also unclear whether lowland hives can stay low in oxygen long enough to stop mites safely. The bees themselves would need to remain unharmed.

Future research could test whether narrowing hive entrances keeps mite numbers down over a full season.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

In a recent development, think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

Industry observers note that intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, states Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

Well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

Industry observers note that “Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys says. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

According to recent reports, first, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

Industry observers note that second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

According to recent reports, sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

Since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

Recent findings suggest that and the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

Your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her company, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

When working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea indicates. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

Recent findings suggest that overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys says. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more key at that point in time.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Today’s Image of the Day looks down on the west coast of Spitsbergen, where glaciers reach the sea and tan streaks cut through turquoise water.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A laser station in Svalbard tracks satellites as they pass over the Arctic, helping scientists measure changes in ice and sea level.

Today’s Image of the Day looks down on the west coast of Spitsbergen, where glaciers reach the sea and tan streaks cut through turquoise water.

Near the shore of one of those fjords, a research station does much of its work in the opposite direction. It aims a laser into the sky to find out exactly where satellites are as they pass overhead.

Landsat 9 captured this view of Norway’s Svalbard archipelago on July 30, 2026.

The laser system at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory officially debuted that October.

It’s the northernmost satellite laser ranging facility in the world, a distinction that matters because of how often some satellites pass within reach.

In a recent development, imagine tracing a line around a globe that passes close to both poles. Turn the globe a little and draw another line along the same path.

In a recent development, the two lines cross the equator far apart, but they come close together in the far north. As Earth rotates beneath a satellite in a near-polar orbit, its path over the ground follows much the same pattern.

Recent findings suggest that that gives Ny-Ålesund more chances to track the same satellite. NASA’s station in Greenbelt, Maryland, might catch a polar-orbiting satellite two or three times a day.

At Ny-Ålesund, a satellite on that kind of route can come within view on almost every orbit.

The Arctic station also fills a geographic gap in a network of more than 40 laser ranging stations around the world.

The station sends a short pulse of light toward a satellite equipped with special reflectors.

Sources indicate that some of that light returns to a detector on the ground. Since scientists know how fast light travels, they can convert the round-trip time to a distance.

Half the total distance traveled is the range from the station to the satellite. A series of those measurements helps researchers work out the satellite’s path.

The new system can send thousands of pulses a second, compared with tens per second for older equipment.

Industry observers note that its detector is sensitive enough to register a single photon, the smallest unit of light. That matters because a satellite may send back only a tiny fraction of the light that leaves the ground.

A faster laser gives the station more chances to collect those faint returns during a pass.

According to recent reports, one satellite that can benefit from the Svalbard station is ICESat-2. It carries a laser of its own and points it down to measure the height of ice sheets, sea ice and other surfaces.

In that case, the satellite times light returning from Earth. At Ny-Ålesund, the station times light returning from the satellite.

The two measurements answer different questions that matter to the same mission.

Recent findings suggest that to see why, imagine measuring the height of a glacier from an aircraft. Knowing the distance down to the ice gets you partway there.

Sources indicate that you also need to know the aircraft’s altitude at the moment of the measurement. The same principle applies in orbit.

A precise record of where ICESat-2 was when it made a reading helps researchers determine the height of the surface below and compare it with measurements from later passes.

Those comparisons depend on a common set of coordinates called the terrestrial reference frame.

It gives scientists a consistent way to describe where objects are on and around Earth, even as the ground itself shifts.

Laser ranging helps maintain that system, so researchers using different instruments in different parts of the world can compare measurements of things like rising seas and moving tectonic plates.

There’s also a local complication for the team in Svalbard. The observatory sits next to a bird sanctuary where access is restricted during the summer breeding season.

The station can operate remotely when staff can’t get to the site, a capability NASA can carry over to future installations.

According to recent reports, the Landsat image gives us one summer view of the fjord. Understanding how the landscape changes takes years of observations that can be lined up and compared.

From a patch of coast in that image, the Ny-Ålesund station helps make those comparisons possible, one pulse of light at a time.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin, using USGS Landsat data.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that newly introduced congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” noted Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the upcoming lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

New maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, remarked he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

According to recent reports, advocates for a upcoming map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley remarked he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

According to recent reports, republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in Fresh York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in New York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Industry observers note that officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass latest maps and could decide to revisit the concern. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where fresh maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, noted last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In Upcoming Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their upcoming majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he stated Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that lake Mead ended September 2026 lower than at any month's end since 1937.
  • Recent findings suggest that on October 22, 2026, the water behind Hoover Dam stood at 1,037.16 feet above sea level.
  • The previous low point of the drought came in July 2022, when the lake ended the month at 1,040.92 feet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that lake Mead ended September 2026 lower than at any month's end since 1937. The Park Service is planning for Temple Bar Marina before a drop expected in spring.

Recent findings suggest that on October 22, 2026, the water behind Hoover Dam stood at 1,037.16 feet above sea level. According to the Bureau of Reclamation’s records, Lake Mead had not been that low since the spring of 1937, when the reservoir was still filling for the first time.

The previous low point of the drought came in July 2022, when the lake ended the month at 1,040.92 feet. This year it finished August, September and October below that mark.

Now the National Park Service (NPS) is preparing for what comes next. On November 20, officials announced that the NPS is developing a low-water strategy for Temple Bar Marina.

It lies on the Arizona side of Lake Mead National Recreation Area, and changes to marina operations are expected in early spring 2027.

At its current location, Temple Bar Marina needs a lake elevation of roughly 1,030 to 1,035 feet to keep running its marina and other water-based services, the park said.

According to the park’s November 20 announcement, Bureau of Reclamation projections show Lake Mead staying between 1,040 and 1,041 feet for the rest of 2026, then falling below 1,020 feet by May 2027.

The Park Service has secured $539,000 for the operations, logistics and visitor services needed to maintain lake access at the marina’s current location down to 1,020 feet as water levels fluctuate.

Below that threshold, the Park Service and the marina’s operator, LMNRA Guest Services, are preparing an orderly transition that includes removing or repositioning marina infrastructure.

“Lake Mead has a long history of adapting to changing conditions while keeping recreational opportunities available to the public,” remarked Ed Clark, the park’s acting superintendent.

According to recent reports, the concessioner will contact affected vessel owners directly about what they may need to do, when, and what options they have. Owners remain responsible for safely removing or relocating their boats as conditions change.

Not everything at Temple Bar depends on the water line. The strategy also covers the land-based services, including lodging, dining and the trailer village, which the operator intends to keep running with reduced staff.

The park is still weighing options for maintaining boat launch access at Temple Bar, in line with its Sustainable Low Water Access Plan, and is asking people who use the area to check its website regularly for updates on the marina and access.

Temple Bar is one of five key locations covered by that initiative, along with Hemenway Harbor, Callville Bay, Echo Bay and South Cove.

In a recent development, when it is full, Lake Mead reaches about 1,220 feet near the dam and holds 9.3 trillion gallons of water, according to NASA’s Earth Observatory. It last came close to full in the summers of 1983 and 1999.

Recent findings suggest that reclamation’s monthly records show how steep the drop has been. At the end of July 2000, the lake stood at 1,199.97 feet. At the end of September 2026, it was about 162 feet lower.

Industry observers note that the pale bands visible along the shoreline in satellite images are mineral deposits on rock that used to be underwater when the reservoir was fuller. They are often called the “bathtub ring.”.

Industry observers note that lake Mead is the largest reservoir in the United States. Most of its water comes from snowmelt in the Rocky Mountains, which flows down the Colorado River through Lake Powell and the Grand Canyon.

Industry observers note that only about 10% comes from local rain and groundwater each year, NASA indicates. Upstream, Lake Powell has fallen to its lowest level ever recorded.

The Colorado River system supplies water and electricity to roughly 40 million people, including the cities of Las Vegas, Phoenix, Los Angeles and San Diego, as well as 4 to 5 million acres of farmland in the Southwest, and the basin is also losing groundwater where scientists least expected.

In November, the lake rose slightly, from 1,038.85 feet at the end of October. By November 20 it stood at 1,041.36 feet, Reclamation’s daily records show.

The bigger question is what happens upstream. In its dry-scenario forecast published on November 16, Reclamation assumed that only 6.21 million acre-feet of water would flow into Lake Powell over the 2027 water year, 65% of average.

Reclamation describes that scenario as a dry condition that, statistically, would be exceeded 90% of the time, meaning inflows would likely be higher in about nine years out of 10.

Even under those assumptions, Lake Mead was projected to end 2026 at 1,040.19 feet.

According to recent reports, the forecast predicts a steep drop in spring 2027. In the same scenario, the lake would fall to 1,032.41 feet by the end of March 2027 and to 1,016.93 feet by the end of May, below the 1,020-foot level down to which the park has funded lake access at the marina.

The Temple Bar strategy builds on the park’s ongoing efforts to keep motorized boating and lake access available on its Arizona side, and any boat launch option must be consistent with the 2023 Sustainable Low Water Access Blueprint and Environmental Assessment.

It has been revealed that for now, the changes to marina operations are not expected until early spring 2027. What happens to the boats will depend on how far the lake falls in the spring.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s announcement on Temple Bar Marina and its page on the Sustainable Low Water Access Proposal, the Bureau of Reclamation’s end-of-month elevations for Lake Mead, its daily reservoir levels and its November 2026 probable minimum 24-Month Study, and NASA Earth Observatory’s Lake Mead Keeps Dropping.

Young adults are turning to AI chatbots to ask about drugs and alcohol

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • About one in three young adults surveyed had asked an AI chatbot about drugs or alcohol, most often to find out what would happen if they used a substance.
  • Industry observers note that about one in three young adults in a recent U.S.
  • Nearly all of the 995 young adults surveyed had used a chatbot like ChatGPT.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About one in three young adults surveyed had asked an AI chatbot about drugs or alcohol, most often to find out what would happen if they used a substance.

Industry observers note that about one in three young adults in a recent U.S. survey had turned to a chatbot with questions about drugs or alcohol. Most wanted to know what would happen if they used a substance.

Nearly all of the 995 young adults surveyed had used a chatbot like ChatGPT.

Of the 321 respondents who asked chatbots about substances, 155 did so at least monthly. Of those, 103 asked once a month, 39 once a week, and 13 daily or almost daily.

Mireia Triguero Roura, a postdoctoral researcher at the Rutgers Institute for Health, Health Care Policy and Aging Research, surveyed 995 Americans aged 18 to 29 in April 2026.

Pia Mauro, an associate professor at the Rutgers School of Public Health, was the co-author.

The respondents were recruited online, and the authors wrote that an online sample may make the habit look more common than it is.

The researchers said the finding concerned them, because the programs behind chatbots can easily reproduce false information.

“Using these tools can lead to misinformed or otherwise risky substance-use behavior among young people, who are the age group most affected by adverse effects of substance use,” Triguero Roura stated.

A 2025 study in JAMA Network Open had found that about one in six young people used a chatbot for mental health advice. How many used one for drug and alcohol questions was unknown until this survey.

Among the 321 respondents who had asked a chatbot about substances, 92.8% wanted to know about the consequences of using one, such as the risks.

In a recent development, about half, 48.6%, asked for specifics about a substance, such as how much to take. Just over a third asked about addiction and related problems.

Sources indicate that the chatbot people were also searching the old way. Of the 321, 298 had looked up substances on Google too, and across the whole survey 57.5% had done a substance-related Google search.

The chatbot was one more source, not a replacement.

Recent findings suggest that the authors gave two reasons the numbers matter. Drugs or alcohol accounted for 25% of deaths among US young adults from 2018 to 2024, according to the federal mortality data they cited.

And news reports have described the overdose death of a young adult who had used a chatbot to learn about substance use.

In a recent development, age made no measurable difference. Respondents aged 18 to 23 and those aged 24 to 29 were about equally likely to have asked, and so were students and non-students. Race and sex did make a difference.

Among the 139 Black respondents, 71 had asked a chatbot about substances, compared with 181 of the 607 white respondents.

In a recent development, men were more likely than women to have asked about substances. Among men, 198 of 497 had asked, compared with 123 of 496 women.

Both gaps held after the researchers accounted for the other characteristics, including age and whether a respondent was a student.

Triguero Roura offered some possible reasons for the gaps, which the study didn’t test.

“The observed disparities in who chooses to use AI for drug-related inquiries could reflect differences in healthcare access, stigma, trust, and health information-seeking behaviors.”.

Prolific, the platform the researchers used to recruit respondents, did not provide information on Hispanic origin, so the researchers could not report results separately for Hispanic young adults.

Recent findings suggest that the 321 chatbot users also rated how helpful, reliable, and trustworthy they found chatbots on a scale of 1 to 5, once for everyday use and once for substance questions. Ratings were high for both.

Helpfulness scored higher for everyday use, 4.44 on the 5-point scale, than for substance questions, 4.12.

Trustworthiness was higher for substance questions, 3.66, than for everyday use, 3.51. Reliability was about the same for both.

So young adults found chatbots a little less helpful on drugs than on everything else, and a little more trustworthy. Anonymity may be part of the appeal, the authors wrote.

They also cited tests of chatbots on health questions that produced concerning results and noted that young adults could act on misinformation a chatbot repeats.

According to recent reports, the researchers recruited respondents in April 2026 through Prolific, an online panel that verifies its participants and pays them for surveys. Each respondent earned 50 cents.

The sample was built to match the US young adult population, including roughly equal numbers of men and women.

The two age groups (18–23 and 24–29) were similar in size, and the racial breakdown was based on census survey figures.

Before asking about substances, the survey described what it meant by generative AI: chatbots or apps that mimic human conversation.

ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Meta AI, and Snap’s My AI were the examples given. Of the 995 people who passed the quality checks, 968 had used one at some point.

The 27 who hadn’t were counted as not having asked about substances. Five more respondents were dropped for failing the checks.

The researchers asked who used chatbots for substance questions, not what the chatbots told them.

Whether the answers were accurate, and what young adults did with them, is the open question, the authors wrote.

The questions were adapted for this survey and hadn’t been tested before, and some answers may be inaccurate despite the quality checks.

Triguero Roura and Mauro wrote that the next studies should test how accurate chatbot answers about substances are, and how young adults interpret and act on them.

According to recent reports, about a third of respondents had asked a chatbot about drugs or alcohol. What those chatbots told them remains an open question.

The full study was published in the journal JMIR Formative Research.

Recent findings suggest that rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., conducts a news conference outside the Capitol on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the concern could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Recent findings suggest that speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

It has been revealed that he must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie mentioned he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

Recent findings suggest that the questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

In a recent development, "It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie noted. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie noted: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries stated. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The Upcoming Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Sources indicate that referring to Massie’s measure, Smith remarked, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

"Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

It has been revealed that also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

According to recent reports, "By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

It has been revealed that massie unveiled in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s latest resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Sources indicate that further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:.

In a recent development, the House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” indicates Yin, of Cornell University.

According to recent reports, he applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin notes, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

Sources indicate that more recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

#88613. Americans Are Rethinking What Comes After Death. For Some, the Answer Is Becoming Soil.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3655 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popularmechanics ↗ Open Full Page

Americans Are Rethinking What Comes After Death. For Some, the Answer Is Becoming Soil.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • In the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed.
  • It has been revealed that some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

In the United States, the way we think about death has rapidly changed. For instance, a 2026 National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA) report predicts that cremation will account for more than 64 percent of funerary arrangements this year. Likewise, an NFDA release from 2025 claims that more than 61 percent of consumers are interested in exploring “green funeral” options.

It has been revealed that some of those people are opting for human composting, or natural organic reduction. It doesn’t require high heat generation, it doesn’t take up space like a traditional burial, and it creates a natural source of plant nutrition. It’s a way to truly return to the earth.

It has been revealed that in a human composting center, workers place a body into a contained ecosystem along with natural bedding like mulch and hay, and periodically tend to each habitat (similar to how you rotate your compost.) The process that Katrina Spade helped to design at her company—Recompose, based in Seattle—is modeled on one used to compost dead livestock; in testing, she hired a soil scientist to ensure that the heat of the composting process was enough to kill any pathogens. This happens in plant and animal composting, too.

It has been revealed that at a similar firm, Return Home, the process digests the soft tissues of the body into nutrients in the soil. Then the bones and any medical devices can be removed, and the latter are recycled. The company uses a cremulator, a traditional cremation tool, to grind bones into pieces. Like a coffee grinder or blender, the cremulator’s rotating blades turn larger pieces into smaller ones. The resulting finer particulate of bone is ideal for composting.

Recent findings suggest that today, people interested in burial have a lot of choices. That’s partly because strict laws and taboos around burying people outside of cemeteries or other designated places are changing. A majority of states allow burial on private property, some with caveats. Embalming is not required across the board. Even the required depth of burial varies a lot, and some states don’t have a depth requirement.

Industry observers note that for some people, allowing unembalmed burial on private land isn’t enough. Many people will never own land in a rural enough place to comfortably bury a loved one. Cemeteries have been running out of space for a while, and experts say fewer people want the traditional American ceremonies linked with death, like viewings and services at funeral homes and churches. But that doesn’t mean people don’t want their death to bring closure, a sense of ritual, or a meaningful return to the earth.

Industry observers note that cities have long had unique challenges with human burial because of their population density. Neighborhoods might eventually surround cemeteries on the edge of town by the time they need to expand. Our parklike modern cemeteries date back to just Victorian times, when they were boosted as part of an overall public park movement in the United Kingdom. Even Brooklyn’s iconic Green-Wood Cemetery started as a public park. But while taxes fund parks, cemeteries are often privately owned. When they stop having open spaces to sell, they start losing income. It grows ethically murky very fast.

This is where human composting enters the scene. As a graduate student, Spade first introduced the idea in her architecture thesis in 2013, The Verge reports. She wondered if people in cities might strategy to send their dead bodies to clean, organized spaces where caretakers could use nature’s own processes to speed up decomposition—or “recomposition,” as she calls it. This results in an amount of enriched soil, because the human body is full of nutrients like nitrogen, potassium, and phosphate that plants need.

In a recent development, it works a lot like any other composting system, or wild life cycle, such as a decomposing log or whale fall—when dead whales sink and become an instant food source for other creatures. Natural topsoil called humus hosts organisms whose place in the ecosystem is to digest animal and plant matter into soil. On the spectrum of humus decomposers, earthworms fall on the larger end, while microbes and tiny insects fall on the smaller end. Together, they form a food web, with each organism playing a part, like digesting a particular nutrient or a particular size of particle.

“Death market” figures show the overall rise in cremation rates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cremation results in a small, tangible object that can be buried anytime, without the countdown to decay that even embalming can’t stop. For decades, the practice has been growing in popularity as a more environmental and space-saving way to prepare bodies after death.

It has been revealed that but that’s not the end of the story. Traditional cremation requires temperatures of 1,400–1,600 Fahrenheit, the Cremation Association of North America explains. The type of ashes we imagine—where what is left is fine powder with some small shards of bone—is just not possible with a wood fire. While it is possible with coal or maybe an accelerant, at that point, the environmental catch-22 is pretty evident. Traditional cremation is better at saving space than it is at saving the planet—and saving space has had enormous value around the world for thousands of years.

In a recent development, the Financial Times estimates that each traditional cremation in the U.K. in 2018 cost about 150 kilograms of carbon dioxide; that’s more than a one-way flight from Boston to Paris. Traditional funerals cost many thousands of dollars on average, and burying embalmed human bodies in airtight containers has never been an environmentally friendly project to begin with. If you’re thinking about your future, there are more options than ever.

Recent findings suggest that at Return Home, the “immediate need” package costs $5,950. The organization also offers another option at the same price: pre-planning your funeral and financing it with a payment initiative. At Recompose, the composting service is $7,000, with options for various remembrance services ranging from $500 up to $1,700. These are somewhat in line with current funeral costs, estimated at an average of $8,596, according to US Funerals Online, an industry resource company based in Delaware.

There’s also one wrinkle if you want your body to be composted after your death: Bodies cannot be embalmed before the process starts. The chemicals used in the funeral industry are “not compatible with” the natural decomposition process, Recompose explains, and many are carcinogenic or otherwise toxic. In other words, they aren’t safe to mix into soil that people will take home and use in their yards. If you die while traveling, you will typically be embalmed before you’re transported home.

In a recent development, there’s an interesting split over human composting, particularly evident in Christianity. The Verge’s 2022 article about Return Home leads with an anecdote about Sharon, a woman who had died from complications of multiple sclerosis. She was also a Mormon. True-blue Christians hew to an idea called stewardship, which is the way humankind must care for the earth and environment as cornerstones of God’s creation.

Sources indicate that and today, that often includes climate change. According to a 2025 survey from Pew Research Center, highly-religious Americans are more likely to believe God gave humans the duty to protect Earth, even in comparison to those who are moderately religious. However, there is also a history of cremation being a contentious issue in Catholicism, though the strictness has relaxed in recent years. Taboos about burial did not stop Sharon, and perhaps won’t stop others who don’t take the resurrection of the body literally. To many people, even those who are Christians, the body is the vessel for what really makes human beings special.

Your reaction to the details above might be a good litmus test for how you feel about human composting. But if you think it sounds disgusting, and to even think about it is macabre—that’s valid! The vast majority of Americans are still choosing traditional burial or cremation. Today, human composting is legal in more than a dozen states, with legislation in the process in several more.

#88612. Tech Report: Petunias reveal an unexpected link between flower color and scent

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1285 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Petunias reveal an unexpected link between flower color and scent

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists studying petunias discovered that the same biological machinery responsible for flower color also shapes their scent.
  • Petunias use the same raw ingredient, an amino acid called phenylalanine, to make pigments and many of their scent compounds.
  • Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem found that a protein called EOBV works with two proteins involved in pigmentation to regulate the flower’s scent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists studying petunias discovered that the same biological machinery responsible for flower color also shapes their scent.

Petunias use the same raw ingredient, an amino acid called phenylalanine, to make pigments and many of their scent compounds.

Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem found that a protein called EOBV works with two proteins involved in pigmentation to regulate the flower’s scent.

When the researchers removed this protein, the flowers released more compounds associated with the smell of cloves and vanilla.

However, they released less methyl benzoate, normally the most abundant scent compound in these petunias.

Oded Skaliter and Alexander Vainstein ran all of it in petunias. The chemistry moved. Nobody has checked whether a nose, human or moth, can tell the difference.

Wild petunias have different ways of attracting pollinators. One species releases its fragrance at night to attract moths, another attracts bees with purple flowers, and a third uses red flowers to attract hummingbirds.

Petunia pigment is run by a committee of three, known to biologists as the MBW complex.

Two of these proteins, AN1 and AN11, remain the same. The third can be any one of several proteins belonging to a family called MYB, and its identity determines which genes the group controls.

Skaliter and his colleagues examined when AN1 and AN11 were most active.

Activity peaked as the flowers opened and remained high for another two days, around the same time that scent production reached its peak.

Industry observers note that then they knocked each gene down, one at a time, with a plant virus. Air from around the petals went into the analyzer.

Recent findings suggest that both treatments increased the release of eugenol and vanillin. The amount of methyl benzoate roughly doubled.

Rather than helping the flowers produce more fragrance, the pigment proteins appeared to hold scent production back.

The researchers suspected that the missing piece of the puzzle was the third protein in the group.

Six MYB proteins were already in the frame here, all of them previously linked to petunia fragrance.

According to recent reports, each went up against AN1 and AN11 in yeast cells that change color when two proteins bind. EOBV was the only hit.

The team repeated the experiment in living plant tissue. This time, they used a system that produces betalain, the red pigment found in beets, when proteins interact.

Recent findings suggest that leaves of a tobacco relative turned red when they received both AN1 and EOBV. Leaves that received AN1 alone produced a weaker color signal.

In a recent development, the strongest red color appeared when all three proteins were present. Removing any one of them greatly reduced pigment production in the test.

According to recent reports, AN11 and EOBV would not bind each other. AN1 had to stand between them.

Industry observers note that the researchers also found very little EOBV gene activity outside the petals. Within the petals, activity was about 1.8 times higher in the upper surface layer, through which fragrance escapes.

Previous work from the same laboratory found that a gene responsible for giving petals their identity also activates scent production.

The next step was to remove EOBV completely. A virus carried CRISPR gene-editing tools into petunia tissue, and the team recovered three groups of edited plants.

Sources indicate that in one group, the instructions for starting the protein were gone, along with the first 42 amino acids. Production in the other two stopped after 58 and 91 amino acids.

The edited plants still looked and flowered like the originals.

Two-day-old flowers then went into sealed jars, two flowers to a jar, and whatever they gave off over the next 24 hours was trapped and measured.

Without a working version of EOBV, the flowers released more eugenol, both forms of isoeugenol and vanillin. These compounds give cloves and vanilla their familiar aromas.

However, the flowers released less of almost every other scent compound, including methyl benzoate. The total amount of fragrance released also fell.

The team then ground up petals to measure how much of each compound remained inside. The clove and vanilla compounds had increased there, too.

The petals contained similar amounts of methyl benzoate and several other scent compounds even though the edited flowers released less of them.

Sources indicate that A repressor has to act on something, so the next question was which genes EOBV holds down. Gene activity was compared between edited and unedited flowers.

Most showed little difference. However, two genes, known as C4H2 and ADT3, became more active after the researchers removed EOBV.

C4H2 controls the carbon supply to the branch that produces eugenol, isoeugenol and vanillin.

The rise in C4H2 gene activity may help explain why the edited flowers made more eugenol, isoeugenol, and vanillin.

The team then tested that link directly. They connected the region of DNA that controls C4H2 activity to a system that produces red pigment.

Recent findings suggest that petals that received EOBV highlighted no visible red color. Petals without the additional EOBV produced more than twice as much pigment.

Two other fragrance genes, PAAS and BSMT, became less active in the edited flowers. Since EOBV does not appear to bind directly to the regions controlling these genes, the changes were probably indirect.

Industry observers note that researchers found a similar pattern in 2011 when they reduced the activity of another petunia gene called PhMYB4. PhMYB4 and EOBV are about 80% identical. Genetic testing confirmed that PhMYB4 itself had not been edited.

EOBV becomes more active when petunias grow in warmer conditions. The researchers wanted to see whether removing it could protect flowers from heat.

They grew the plants in a greenhouse for a month before moving them into two rooms. The cooler room had temperatures of 72°F (22°C) during the day and 61°F (16°C) at night. The warmer room reached 82°F (28°C) and 72°F (22°C), respectively.

After measuring 38 flowers, the team found that unedited flowers became 12% narrower in warmer conditions. Edited flowers shrank by only 6%.

Heat also reduced the amount of scent released by unedited flowers, mainly due to lower emissions of benzaldehyde and methyl benzoate. Edited flowers maintained their overall scent output.

Meanwhile, PhEXP1, a gene that helps petal cells expand, became less active in both groups by similar amounts.

Heat-shrunk petunia flowers were traced to slower cell division in a 2021 study, a step this team did not measure.

More vanilla and clove compounds might sound appealing, but would these petunias actually smell better?

Nobody has asked people to smell the edited flowers. The researchers haven’t tested pollinators either.

Removing EOBV also has limits. In purple varieties, reducing EOBV activity left pigment levels unchanged.

EOBV belongs to the color machinery without fixing the shade of purple itself.

Industry observers note that the team also crossed the edited plants with petunias lacking EVER, another scent regulator. Those flowers did not outperform either parent. The authors suggest limited carbon, or a limited capacity to release scent.

According to recent reports, the authors also disclosed a commercial interest. Skaliter and Vainstein are chief technology officer and chief scientific officer at CapsiBreed, which uses gene editing in hot and sweet peppers. Peppers and petunias are relatives.

One obvious next experiment is to switch EOBV off in plants that are already missing AN1 or AN11.

In a recent development, the team also wants to know whether other flowering plants are wired this way. And growers will want an answer to a blunter question: does a reshuffled scent give them flowers that anyone wants to buy?

The full study was published in the journal Plant Physiology.

#88610. Sitting behind the wheel may do something unusual to your heart rate

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1391 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Sitting behind the wheel may do something unusual to your heart rate

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Driving keeps the heart above its resting rate for longer, even when the body remains seated and inactive.
  • Sitting behind the wheel is usually treated as no different from sitting anywhere else.
  • Recent findings suggest that during the time these people spent driving, their heart rates remained above resting level almost throughout.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Driving keeps the heart above its resting rate for longer, even when the body remains seated and inactive.

Sitting behind the wheel is usually treated as no different from sitting anywhere else. Heart-rate readings that were collected for a week from 57 young adults in Texas now suggest otherwise.

Recent findings suggest that during the time these people spent driving, their heart rates remained above resting level almost throughout. A return to resting level was recorded about half as often as during other inactive hours.

In a recent development, their hearts were not found to beat faster in the car than during those other hours. The resting pace was simply reached less often while a person was driving.

The study was designed and supervised by Ioannis Pavlidis who is a computer science professor at the University of Houston.

Colleagues from the same university and from the Texas A&M Transportation Institute worked with him.

Pavlidis said that a driver has to keep watching the road and deciding what to do next.

In a recent development, “The body may be sitting, but the mind is working,” he said. According to him, it is in the heart rate that this mental work can be seen.

What the study isn’t able to show is that driving itself kept anyone’s heart rate up. The comparison that was made was between time spent driving and other inactive time in one week.

There are more differences between these two kinds of time than the car alone.

Posture and caffeine are on the list of them that the authors gave and so are passengers. How urgently a driver needed to arrive is on that list as well.

The group consisted of 30 men and 27 women with an average age of about 26. Most of them were office workers.

A personal iPhone and Apple Watch were used by each participant from Monday through Sunday.

Every car was fitted with a small plug-in device by which each period of driving could be recorded. The watch was the source of the heart rate readings to which weather and traffic conditions were matched.

The rest of each day was labeled with the help of activity data from the phone and the watch. Any recorded minute in which a person was neither driving nor physically active was taken into the comparison.

Such minutes may have been spent at work or at home or somewhere else entirely.

Industry observers note that the batteries of the iPhone and Apple Watch had usually run out by early evening. It is for this reason that the recordings cover daytime hours alone.

It was Pavlidis’ group at the Affective and Data Computing Laboratory that averaged the readings minute by minute. The recordings that resulted came to 177,318 minutes which is close to 3,000 hours.

It has been revealed that no heart-rate reading existed for 13.6% of the driving minutes or for 3.5% of other inactive minutes. Neither speed nor traffic was found to be linked to the readings that were missing.

Recent findings suggest that driving took up about a tenth of that time. There were 973 trips in total and half of them were over within 15 minutes. A crash or a traffic ticket was generally not part of these drives.

Before any single minute could be judged, the team had to know each person’s resting heart rate.

An estimate of it is produced by the Apple Watch once a day. These daily estimates were averaged by the team across the whole week.

According to recent reports, while a person was driving, their heart rate was above their own resting level 93.7% of the time on average. The figure for other inactive time was 81.3%.

Yet a higher heart rate in the car was not what the Houston team found. During driving, it averaged 11.2 beats per minute above resting level. The average for other inactive time was 11.5 beats above resting level.

A gap as small as that could have come up by chance.

According to recent reports, where driving did differ was in how little the heart rate varied. Its typical spread was 7.98 beats per minute during driving and 12.40 beats during other inactive time.

Heart rates dropped to resting level 2.46 times per hour during other inactive time and 1.31 times per hour while driving.

On weekdays, the two shares of time above resting level were 93.8% and 82.1%.

Weekends showed the same pattern, although people then spend their hours outside the car differently.

According to Pavlidis, a workout also raises heart rate, but the body becomes fitter as a result of it. From the time that is spent behind the wheel, no benefit of that kind is gained.

Yasmine Bouzid and the other authors also examined what a higher or lower heart rate was tied to.

According to recent reports, during driving, there were two things that stood out from the rest. Time of day was the first since heart rates were higher in drives after noon than in the morning.

The second was the amount by which the driver’s wrist had turned in the minute before. The gyroscope of the Apple Watch supplied this measure which was treated as a sign of steering.

In a recent development, away from the car, the list that was found was a broader one. On it were age and sex along with time of day and the Big Five personality trait of openness.

In a recent development, for this, the authors offered one reason which they regarded as possible. Driving is a single task whose demands remain fairly steady from one minute to the next.

Many different situations are covered by the inactive time that is spent away from the car.

Because a drive is repeated day after day, an example using anxiety was worked through by the team.

The volunteers had filled out the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, which scores a tendency to feel anxious from 20 to 80. The lowest score that was found in this group was 20 while the highest was 61.

Sources indicate that over every recorded minute of driving, the team’s heart-rate model was then run twice. A score of 20 was given to every driver in the first of these runs. In the second run, it was a score of 61 that every driver was given.

The heart rate that the model predicted with the score of 61 was higher by 0.99 beats per minute.

What the Houston team then did was to count such beats over a whole year. For a person who drives eight hours a day, the model projected about 173,000 extra heartbeats.

It came to roughly 11,000 extra heartbeats when the same was done for a 30-minute daily drive.

According to recent reports, it was only as illustrations that these totals were described by Pavlidis and his coauthors. What they show is how a small difference accumulates, and not what anyone’s risk of heart disease is.

There were only young adults from Texas among the 57 volunteers, and none was followed for more than a week. Older drivers, professional drivers, or people with heart disease may not show the results that were found here.

It will take years of following drivers before the health side of this can be judged. Only then can it be learned whether more time above resting heart rate predicts heart problems.

In a recent development, pavlidis said that driving is something many people can’t do without. What his lab in Houston wants to find out is how the same trips could be made less demanding.

The Texas A&M Transportation Institute, where study co-author Michael Manser works, is supporting the lab through 2027.

The people who are to be studied next include long-distance commuters and those who drive for a living.

In a recent development, rideshare drivers are an example of the latter. The groups are meant to be bigger, more varied, and followed for longer.

There is one more question that self-driving cars from Waymo and Tesla have raised for the lab. What does a rider’s heart rate do when it is the vehicle that handles the driving?

The full study was published in the journal npj Digital Public Health.

How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina
